title: Working on the Cluster with Red Spruce Fitness-Trait Data
text:
This tutorial walks through a small, reproducible high-performance computing (HPC) workflow using a public red spruce fitness-trait dataset. Rather than receiving a copy of the data by email or flash drive, you will download the source file into your project directory, inspect it from the command line, analyze it in R, and submit that R analysis to Slurm.
The source file is FitnessTraits_GeneticParameters_RedSpruce.txt from the Genomic_assisted_selection repository. The repository supports the manuscript Bringing genomics to the field: An integrative approach to seed sourcing for forest restoration.

title: Working on the Cluster with Red Spruce Fitness-Trait Data
text:
This tutorial walks through a small, reproducible high-performance computing (HPC) workflow using a public red spruce fitness-trait dataset. Rather than receiving a copy of the data by email or flash drive, you will download the source file into your project directory, inspect it from the command line, analyze it in R, and submit that R analysis to Slurm.
The source file is FitnessTraits_GeneticParameters_RedSpruce.txt from the Genomic_assisted_selection repository. The repository supports the manuscript Bringing genomics to the field: An integrative approach to seed sourcing for forest restoration.

title: Working on the Cluster with Red Spruce Fitness-Trait Data
text:
Learning objectives
By the end, you should be able to:

Navigate a cluster filesystem with bash.
Organize a project using reproducible relative paths.
Download a tab-delimited data file with curl.
Inspect a file with head, less, grep, and wc.
Run an R script interactively and non-interactively.
Submit and monitor a simple Slurm job with sbatch and squeue.
Locate output tables, figures, and job logs.

title: Working on the Cluster with Red Spruce Fitness-Trait Data
text:
Project setup
Log in to your cluster, then create a dedicated project directory:
cd ~
pwd

mkdir -p projects/red-spruce-cluster-exercise/{data/raw,results,logs,scripts}
cd ~/projects/red-spruce-cluster-exercise

pwd
ls -R
Your project should have this structure:
red-spruce-cluster-exercise/
├── data/
│   └── raw/       # downloaded, unchanged source data
├── logs/          # Slurm standard output and error logs
├── results/       # analysis products created by R
└── scripts/       # R and Slurm scripts
Using a consistent project structure makes your paths portable. For example, data/raw/red_spruce_traits.txt works for anyone who has the project folder, whereas /home/your_username/... works only on your account and only on one system.

title: Working on the Cluster with Red Spruce Fitness-Trait Data
text:
Download the data
Download the raw GitHub file directly into data/raw/:
curl -L \
  -o data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anoobvinu07/Genomic_assisted_selection/master/data/FitnessTraits_GeneticParameters_RedSpruce.txt
The -L flag tells curl to follow redirects, and -o specifies the local output file. Verify the download before doing any analysis:
ls -lh data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt
head -n 5 data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt
This is a tab-delimited text file. Print the header with one field per line to inspect its variable names:
head -n 1 data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt | tr '\t' '\n'
Other useful checks are:
# Count total lines, including the header
wc -l data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt

# View the complete file interactively; press q to quit
less data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt

# Search for a known trait, population, family, or other text value
# Replace SEARCH_TERM with a value that occurs in the data.
grep "SEARCH_TERM" data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt | head






NoteCheckpoint



Before continuing, identify the data-file header, count the total lines, and write down two variables you expect to be numeric. Do not assume a column’s type from its name alone: check the data.

title: Working on the Cluster with Red Spruce Fitness-Trait Data
text:
Create an R script
Create a script using a terminal editor:
nano scripts/analyze_red_spruce.R
Paste the following code. It uses base R only, so it does not require installing packages. The script detects numeric variables, writes a descriptive-statistics table, creates a correlation matrix, and makes a histogram for the first numeric variable it finds.
#!/usr/bin/env Rscript

input_file <- "data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt"
results_dir <- "results"

if (!file.exists(input_file)) {
  stop(
    "Input file not found: ", input_file,
    "\nDownload the data first, from the project root."
  )
}

if (!dir.exists(results_dir)) {
  dir.create(results_dir, recursive = TRUE)
}

red_spruce <- read.table(
  input_file,
  header = TRUE,
  sep = "\t",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE
)

cat("Rows:", nrow(red_spruce), "\n")
cat("Columns:", ncol(red_spruce), "\n\n")
cat("Column names:\n")
print(names(red_spruce))
cat("\nFirst six rows:\n")
print(head(red_spruce))

numeric_vars <- names(red_spruce)[vapply(red_spruce, is.numeric, logical(1))]
cat("\nNumeric variables:\n")
print(numeric_vars)

if (length(numeric_vars) == 0) {
  stop("No numeric variables were detected. Inspect the file delimiter and header.")
}

trait_summary <- data.frame(
  variable = numeric_vars,
  n_nonmissing = vapply(red_spruce[numeric_vars], function(x) sum(!is.na(x)), numeric(1)),
  mean = vapply(red_spruce[numeric_vars], function(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), numeric(1)),
  sd = vapply(red_spruce[numeric_vars], function(x) sd(x, na.rm = TRUE), numeric(1)),
  minimum = vapply(red_spruce[numeric_vars], function(x) min(x, na.rm = TRUE), numeric(1)),
  maximum = vapply(red_spruce[numeric_vars], function(x) max(x, na.rm = TRUE), numeric(1))
)

write.csv(
  trait_summary,
  file.path(results_dir, "red_spruce_numeric_summary.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)

if (length(numeric_vars) >= 2) {
  correlation_matrix <- cor(
    red_spruce[numeric_vars],
    use = "pairwise.complete.obs"
  )

  write.csv(
    correlation_matrix,
    file.path(results_dir, "red_spruce_numeric_correlations.csv")
  )
}

first_trait <- numeric_vars[1]
pdf(file.path(results_dir, "first_numeric_trait_histogram.pdf"), width = 7, height = 5)
hist(
  red_spruce[[first_trait]],
  main = paste("Distribution of", first_trait),
  xlab = first_trait,
  col = "grey80",
  border = "white"
)
dev.off()

cat("\nCreated files:\n")
print(list.files(results_dir, full.names = TRUE))
Save in nano with Ctrl + O, press Enter, then exit with Ctrl + X.

title: Working on the Cluster with Red Spruce Fitness-Trait Data
text:
Run R on the terminal
First, determine which R modules are available on your cluster:
module avail R
Load an available version; for example:
module load R/4.3.0
Run the script from the project root:
Rscript scripts/analyze_red_spruce.R
ls -lh results
You can also start an interactive R session for exploration:
R
Then run:
red_spruce <- read.table(
  "data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt",
  header = TRUE,
  sep = "\t"
)

str(red_spruce)
summary(red_spruce)
Exit R with:
q()

title: Working on the Cluster with Red Spruce Fitness-Trait Data
text:
Submit the analysis with Slurm
Create a Slurm submission script:
nano scripts/run_red_spruce.sbatch
Paste this content. Change the R module and --partition to names supported by your cluster.
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=red_spruce
#SBATCH --output=logs/red_spruce_%j.out
#SBATCH --error=logs/red_spruce_%j.err
#SBATCH --time=00:10:00
#SBATCH --partition=standard
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --mem=2G

set -euo pipefail

module load R/4.3.0

# Run relative paths from the directory where sbatch was issued.
cd "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"
mkdir -p results logs

echo "Job ID: ${SLURM_JOB_ID}"
echo "Host: $(hostname)"
echo "Started: $(date)"
echo "Working directory: $(pwd)"

Rscript scripts/analyze_red_spruce.R

echo "Finished: $(date)"
Submit and monitor your job:
sbatch scripts/run_red_spruce.sbatch
squeue -u "$USER"
After the job has completed, replace <JOBID> with the number returned by sbatch:
cat logs/red_spruce_<JOBID>.out
cat logs/red_spruce_<JOBID>.err
ls -lh results

title: Working on the Cluster with Red Spruce Fitness-Trait Data
text:
Exercises

Explain why raw data are saved in data/raw/ and should not be altered by the analysis script.
Use head, less, and grep to inspect the source data before opening R.
Identify what files the R script writes to results/.
Deliberately run the R script from the wrong directory. Read the error, then explain why the project-relative input path fails.
Edit the R script to make a histogram for a different numeric variable.
After inspecting names(red_spruce), create a plot that is biologically meaningful for two variables in this dataset.
Add a README.md containing the GitHub source URL, date accessed, and exact curl command used to obtain the data.

title: Working on the Cluster with Red Spruce Fitness-Trait Data
text:
Take-home message
A reproducible cluster workflow separates source data, scripts, outputs, and logs. Downloading a documented raw-data copy into a project, using relative paths, and running the same script interactively and through Slurm are habits that scale from a small teaching exercise to genomic and quantitative-genetic analyses.

title: Anoob Prakash
text:
A little bit about me
I’m a plant biologist and forest genomicist who spends a lot of time thinking about how trees will cope with a rapidly changing climate. I work at the intersection of ecological and evolutionary genomics, climate science, and data science, using large genomic and environmental datasets to understand – and hopefully help guide – the future of forests.

title: Anoob Prakash
text:
What I work on
Most of my research asks a simple but hard question: how will tree species respond to climate change, and what can we do about it?






NotePhD life





During my PhD at the University of Vermont with Dr. Stephen R. Keller, I focused on red spruce (Picea rubens Sarg.). I combined genomics, climate data, and trait measurements from common gardens to study genotypic and phenotypic variation, local adaptation, and the role of introgression with black spruce (Picea mariana). Along the way, I managed three common gardens, ran GWAS to identify adaptive loci, and spent a lot of time turning messy datasets into interpretable stories.









NoteCollaboration with TNC and CASRI





PhD research work led to collaborations with The Nature Conservancy (TNC) and the Central Appalachian Spruce Restoration Initiative (CASRI). Together, we used genomic information to select seed sources for restoration in the southern range edge of red spruce, which ultimately informed the planting of ~58,000 seedlings across West Virginia, Virginia, and Maryland. It was a satisfying example of science’s real world impact. Read more in the research section

title: Anoob Prakash
text:
What I’m doing now
I’m currently a postdoctoral researcher at Purdue University, working with Dr. Matthew Ginzel and Dr. Vikram Chhatre. Here, I’m using population genetics to understand climate change adaptation in black walnut, white oak, and short leaf pine – species with high restoration potential and major ecological and economic importance.






NoteMore





I use machine‑learning approaches to detect climate pre‑adaptation and mal‑adaptation, and to identify seed sources that are likely to perform well in future climates. A big goal of this work is to provide actionable guidance to practitioners so restoration and reforestation projects can make informed, climate‑savvy seed sourcing decisions.

title: Anoob Prakash
text:
Where I’m coming from
Before moving into conifers and temperate forests, my master’s work in India focused on something more immediate and local: particulate pollution.






NoteEarly days of research





I studied how dust pollution affects growth, physiology, and wood anatomy of moist deciduous tree species, and which species might be more resilient near the Walayar Cement Factory, for my master’s research. That early work shaped my interest in how environmental stressors leave signatures in plant physiology.

title: Anoob Prakash
text:
What I’m trained in






NoteNSF Traineeship





Over the years, I’ve also invested heavily in data skills and open, quantitative science. As an NSF Research Trainee in the Biological Data Science (BilDS) program (formerly QuEST), I collaborated across disciplines at UVM and learned to use quantitative tools to tackle environmental and global health questions. As part of this program, I interned with TNC on large‑scale reforestation planning, which closely aligned with my dissertation work and showed me how genomic data can support real‑world decisions.









NoteUSDA Climate Scholar





I was also a USDA GradCAMP Climate scholar, participating in a year‑long, cohort‑based experience focused on climate adaptation, mitigation, and climate justice. That year involved interdisciplinary research, networking with climate professionals, and science communication, including developing “forests of the future” factsheets. At UVM, I served two years as a graduate student senator for Plant Biology, working on issues related to graduate stipends, mental health, and governance.

title: Anoob Prakash
text:
What I care about
Scientifically, I’m drawn to climate change adaptation, population and landscape genomics, environmental data science, and transparent, reproducible workflows. I enjoy projects that sit at the interface of fundamental evolutionary questions and applied conservation or restoration decisions.






NoteFun side of things





Outside of research, you’ll usually find me on a basketball court, tinkering with data visualizations, learning new illustration tools, or playing games. I enjoy the creative side of science communication – turning complex models and genomic results into visuals and narratives that are intuitive for both scientists and non‑scientists.

title: Adaptation and response to environmental change
section: Red spruce restoration in collaboration with CASRI and TNC
text:
Red spruce restoration in collaboration with CASRI and TNC
Kathryn Shallows from TNC approached the Keller lab in 2019 regarding red spruce restoration towards the southern range edge of its distribution, mainly in Maryland, Virginia and West Virginia. This led to a larger partnership that culminated in genomic assisted seed source selection for the restoration initiative at these sites. Instead of opting for a single source restoration initiative, we used a multiple seed source approach to improve the genetic diversity of the restoration stands to withstand the changing climate and environmental stressors. This source selection was carried out in the light of research done on red spruce using the exome capture data and the common gardens set up at Vermont, Maryland and North Carolina. Three to four sources combinations per restoration site were selected for high genetic diversity and low genetic load.

title: Adaptation and response to environmental change
section: Seed sources: No one for all
text:
Seed sources: No one for all
Capblancq et al. (2021) has observed that early-life fitness of the red spruce had strong positive association with genetic diversity and negative association with genetic load, especially for the southern range edge of the red spruce distribution range. These seed source combinations were used as a recommendation list to Dave Seville (CASRI) to assess the seed production situation on the ground and raise them in the nursery for the restoration initiative. In 2021, TNC planted 58,000 red spruce seedlings at the restoration sites. Keller lab then carried out the restoration monitoring of these restoration sites in 2022, a whole year after the seedlings had been planted in the ground to assess the success of genomic assisted restoration of red spruce. Using this information, Prakash et al. (2024) found that there were no “Super Seed Source” that outperformed other seed sources and the combination of seed sources outperformed any single source for the restoration success.

title: Anoob Prakash
text:
A little bit about me
I’m a plant biologist and forest genomicist who spends a lot of time thinking about how trees will cope with a rapidly changing climate. I work at the intersection of ecological and evolutionary genomics, climate science, and data science, using large genomic and environmental datasets to understand – and hopefully help guide – the future of forests.


What I work on
Most of my research asks a simple but hard question: how will tree species respond to climate change, and what can we do about it?
During my PhD at the University of Vermont with Dr. Stephen R. Keller, I focused on red spruce (Picea rubens Sarg.). I combined genomics, climate data, and trait measurements from common gardens to study genotypic and phenotypic variation, local adaptation, and the role of introgression with black spruce (Picea mariana). Along the way, I managed three common gardens, ran GWAS to identify adaptive loci, and spent a lot of time turning messy datasets into interpretable stories.
That work led to collaborations with The Nature Conservancy (TNC) and Central Appalachian Spruce Restoration initiative (CASRI). Together, we used genomic information to select seed sources for restoration in the southern range edge of red spruce, which ultimately informed the planting of ~58,000 seedlings across West Virginia, Virginia, and Maryland. It was a satisfying example of science’s real world impact.


What I’m doing now
I’m currently a postdoctoral researcher at Purdue University, working with Dr. Matthew Ginzel and Dr. Vikram Chhatre. Here, I’m extending the same ideas to black walnut, white oak, and shortleaf pine – species with high restoration potential and major ecological and economic importance. I use machine-learning approaches to detect climate pre‑adaptation and mal‑adaptation, and to identify seed sources that are likely to perform well in future climates. A big goal of this work is to provide actionable guidance to practitioners so restoration and reforestation projects can make informed, climate‑savvy seed sourcing decisions.


Where I’m coming from
Before moving into conifers and temperate forests, my master’s work in India focused on something more immediate and local: particulate pollution. Near the Walayar Cement Factory, I studied how dust pollution affects growth, physiology, and wood anatomy of moist deciduous tree species, and which species might be more resilient. That early work shaped my interest in how environmental stressors leave signatures in plant physiology.
Over the years, I’ve also invested heavily in data skills and open, quantitative science. As an NSF Research Trainee in the Biological Data Science (BilDS) program (formerly QuEST), I collaborated across disciplines at UVM and learned to use quantitative tools to tackle environmental and global health questions. As part of this program, I interned with TNC on large‑scale reforestation planning, which closely aligned with my dissertation work and showed me how genomic data can support real‑world decisions.
I was also a USDA GradCAMP Climate scholar, participating in a year-long, cohort-based experience focused on climate adaptation, mitigation, and climate justice. That year involved interdisciplinary research, networking with climate professionals, and science communication, including developing “forests of the future” factsheets. At UVM, I served two years as a graduate student senator for Plant Biology, working on issues related to graduate stipends, mental health, and governance.


What I care about
Scientifically, I’m drawn to climate change adaptation, population and landscape genomics, environmental data science, and transparent, reproducible workflows. I enjoy projects that sit at the interface of fundamental evolutionary questions and applied conservation or restoration decisions.
Outside of research, you’ll usually find me on a basketball court, tinkering with data visualizations, learning new illustration tools, or playing games. I enjoy the creative side of science communication – turning complex models and genomic results into visuals and narratives that are intuitive for both scientists and non‑scientists.

title: Getting started with bash on HPC
text:
Cluster exercise: Download and analyze public red-spruce fitness-trait data
In this exercise you will create a reproducible project on the cluster, download a tab-delimited red-spruce dataset directly from a public GitHub repository and inspect it with bash.
The source file is FitnessTraits_GeneticParameters_RedSpruce.txt from the GitHub repository. The repository supports a published manuscript Bringing genomics to the field: An integrative approach to seed sourcing for forest restoration.


By the end, you should be able to:

Navigate a cluster filesystem with bash.
Organize a project using reproducible relative paths.
Download a tab-delimited data file with curl.
Inspect a file with head, less, grep, and wc.

title: Getting started with bash on HPC
text:
Project setup
Step 1: Log in to your cluster, then create a dedicated project directory:

cd ~ # change directory [cd] to home [~]
pwd  # get the present working directory [pwd]
mkdir projects 
This makes a directory (mkdir) or folder at the current location titled “projects”
cd projects # move inside the projects directory
Step 2: Create sub folders under the project folder
mkdir -p cluster-exercise/{data/raw,results,logs,src}
In order to create multiple directories at the same time you can use :

-p : Create directory/directories
{folder-1/subfolder,folder-2,folder-3} : Name of the multiple directory/directories [folders and sub-folders] at the same time







Warning



Do not add spaces between the names {folder-1/subfolder,folder-2,folder-3}
This would disrupt the naming convention



Step 3: Move inside the working directory cluster-exercise and check the layout






TipHow to?



Before we download the data, move inside working directory- which would be the cluster-exercise directory. How do you do that?
Hint: You need to change directory inside cluster-exercise directory


If you are in the right folder on your home (~) directory then run pwd in the terminal. The path would be something like this: /home/alias/projects/cluster-exercise where alias would be your username on the cluster.
Once inside the ‘cluster-exercise’ directory, check the directory layout with tree
tree
Your project should have this structure:
cluster-exercise/
├── data/
│   └── raw/       # downloaded, unchanged source data
├── logs/          # Slurm standard output and error logs
├── results/       # analysis products created by R
└── src/           # R and Slurm scripts
Using a consistent project structure makes your paths portable. For example, data/raw/red_spruce_traits.txt works for anyone who has the project folder, whereas /home/your_username/... works only on your account and only on one system.

Bash quick reference








Command
Purpose
Example




~
Your home directory
cd ~


/
Filesystem root and path separator
cd /scratch


pwd
Print working directory
pwd


ls
List files and directories
ls -lh results


cd
Change directory
cd data/raw


cd ..
Move up one directory
cd ..


mkdir -p
Create directory/directories
mkdir -p logs results


head
Show the beginning of a file
head -n 5 file.txt


less
View a file interactively; press q to exit
less file.txt


grep
Search for text in a file
grep "value" file.txt


wc -l
Count lines
wc -l file.txt


curl -L -o
Download URL into a named file
curl -L -o file.txt URL

title: Getting started with bash on HPC
text:
Download the data

Step 1: Download the raw GitHub file directly into data/raw/
Copy the code below and run it inside the cluster-exercise directory
curl -L \
  -o data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anoobvinu07/Genomic_assisted_selection/master/data/FitnessTraits_GeneticParameters_RedSpruce.txt
The -L flag tells curl to follow redirects, and -o specifies the local output file. Verify the download before doing any analysis:






NoteHow to use curl



curl -L -o location/path/for-download url-of-an-online-data.file

curl is a tool for transferring data from or to a server using URLs
-L is the location of the file and allows redirects if the file is moved
-o writes an output to a given file instead of a standardard output

more details…


Step 2: Check if the files were downloaded correctly Check the file exists with ls - ls : list files inside a directory
- lh : list them in a human readable form
ls -lh data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt
head -n 5 data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt
This is a tab-delimited text file. Print the header with one field per line to inspect its variable names:
head -n 1 data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt | tr '\t' '\n'






TipThings to understand



What does tr do in the command above?
The | in the command is a called a pipe. What does it do?


Step 3: Explore the data
Count the total lines present in the file, including the header.

wc -l data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt
View the file with cat.
cat data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt
That is too much data to look at. Lets just peek at the header for the file.
head data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt
View the complete file interactively; press q to quit.
less data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt
Search for a known trait, population, family, or other text value.

Replace SEARCH_TERM with a value that occurs in the data.

Lets search for the population ALB in the data set.

grep "SEARCH_TERM" data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt | head






TipCan you find the how many families/individuals are from VT (Vermont) location?



Hint!
1. Break it down into individual steps.
2. Then combine them together with pipes.








NoteWrap Up



Before continuing, identify the data-file header, count the total lines, and write down two variables you expect to be numeric. Do not assume a column’s type from its name alone: check the data.

title: Github actions
text:
Create cross-account token
Because the action runs in anoobvinu07/anoobvinu07.github.io but needs to commit to a different repository/account, create a fine-grained personal access token from the anoobprakash GitHub account:

Repository access: Only select anoobprakash/anoobprakash.github.io
Repository permissions: Contents: Read and write

Then, in the source repository (anoobvinu07/anoobvinu07.github.io):

Go to Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions
Create a repository secret named ANOO_B_PAGES_TOKEN
Paste the token.

The workflow’s built-in GITHUB_TOKEN is normally limited to the repository containing the workflow, so it is not suitable for pushing to the other repository.45

title: Github actions
text:
Mirror workflow
Create this file in the source repository:
.github/workflows/mirror-anoobprakash-pages.yml
name: Mirror rendered site to anoobprakash.github.io

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
    paths:
      - "docs/**"
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  mirror-site:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Check out source repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Check out destination repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          repository: anoobprakash/anoobprakash.github.io
          token: ${{ secrets.ANOO_B_PAGES_TOKEN }}
          path: destination

      - name: Copy rendered docs site
        run: |
          mkdir -p destination/docs
          rsync -av --delete \
            --exclude=".git" \
            docs/ destination/docs/

      - name: Commit and push changes
        working-directory: destination
        run: |
          git config user.name "github-actions[bot]"
          git config user.email "41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"

          git add docs/

          if git diff --cached --quiet; then
            echo "No mirrored site changes to commit."
          else
            git commit -m "Mirror website from anoobvinu07"
            git push origin main
          fi

title: Github actions
text:
Important details

paths: ["docs/**"] means the workflow runs only when your rendered website changes, not every time you edit source .qmd files without rendering.
rsync --delete makes the target docs/ an exact mirror. For example, deleting a post or image from the source docs/ also deletes it from the target site.
The target repository may contain other files—such as a README.md or .github/ workflows—because the workflow modifies only destination/docs/.
Add a docs/.nojekyll file to the source repository if it does not already exist. This prevents GitHub Pages from applying Jekyll processing to your already-built Quarto static files. GitHub notes that this is useful for sites built with static site generators other than Jekyll.6

touch docs/.nojekyll
git add docs/.nojekyll
git commit -m "Disable Jekyll processing for Pages"
git push
After you render locally and push the updated docs/ folder to main, the action will update anoobprakash/anoobprakash.github.io/docs/, and GitHub Pages will redeploy that mirrored version automatically. 78910111213141516

title: Getting started with bash on HPC
text:
Cluster exercise: Download and analyze public red-spruce fitness-trait data
In this exercise you will create a reproducible project on the cluster, download a tab-delimited red-spruce dataset directly from a public GitHub repository and inspect it with bash.
The source file is FitnessTraits_GeneticParameters_RedSpruce.txt from the GitHub repository. The repository supports a published manuscript Bringing genomics to the field: An integrative approach to seed sourcing for forest restoration.


By the end, you should be able to:

Navigate a cluster filesystem with bash.
Organize a project using reproducible relative paths.
Download a tab-delimited data file with curl.
Inspect a file with head, less, grep, and wc.

title: Getting started with bash on HPC
text:
Project setup
Step 1: Log in to your cluster, then create a dedicated project directory:

cd ~ # change directory [cd] to home [~]
pwd  # get the present working directory [pwd]
mkdir projects 
This makes a directory (mkdir) or folder at the current location titled “projects”
cd projects # move inside the projects directory
Step 2: Create sub folders under the project folder
mkdir -p cluster-exercise/{data/raw,results,logs,src}
In order to create multiple directories at the same time you can use :

-p : Create directory/directories
{folder-1/subfolder,folder-2,folder-3} : Name of the multiple directory/directories [folders and sub-folders] at the same time







Warning



Do not add spaces between the names {folder-1/subfolder,folder-2,folder-3}
This would disrupt the naming convention



Step 3: Move inside the working directory cluster-exercise and check the layout






TipHow to?



Before we download the data, move inside working directory- which would be the cluster-exercise directory. How do you do that?
Hint: You need to change directory inside cluster-exercise directory


If you are in the right folder on your home (~) directory then run pwd in the terminal. The path would be something like this: /home/alias/projects/cluster-exercise where alias would be your username on the cluster.
Once inside the ‘cluster-exercise’ directory, check the directory layout with tree
tree
Your project should have this structure:
cluster-exercise/
├── data/
│   └── raw/       # downloaded, unchanged source data
├── logs/          # Slurm standard output and error logs
├── results/       # analysis products created by R
└── src/           # R and Slurm scripts
Using a consistent project structure makes your paths portable. For example, data/raw/red_spruce_traits.txt works for anyone who has the project folder, whereas /home/your_username/... works only on your account and only on one system.

Bash quick reference








Command
Purpose
Example




~
Your home directory
cd ~


/
Filesystem root and path separator
cd /scratch


pwd
Print working directory
pwd


ls
List files and directories
ls -lh results


cd
Change directory
cd data/raw


cd ..
Move up one directory
cd ..


mkdir -p
Create directory/directories
mkdir -p logs results


head
Show the beginning of a file
head -n 5 file.txt


less
View a file interactively; press q to exit
less file.txt


grep
Search for text in a file
grep "value" file.txt


wc -l
Count lines
wc -l file.txt


curl -L -o
Download URL into a named file
curl -L -o file.txt URL

title: Getting started with bash on HPC
text:
Download the data

Step 1: Download the raw GitHub file directly into data/raw/
Copy the code below and run it inside the cluster-exercise directory
curl -L \
  -o data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anoobvinu07/Genomic_assisted_selection/master/data/FitnessTraits_GeneticParameters_RedSpruce.txt
The -L flag tells curl to follow redirects, and -o specifies the local output file. Verify the download before doing any analysis:






NoteHow to use curl



curl -L -o location/path/for-download url-of-an-online-data.file

curl is a tool for transferring data from or to a server using URLs
-L is the location of the file and allows redirects if the file is moved
-o writes an output to a given file instead of a standardard output

more details…


Step 2: Check if the files were downloaded correctly Check the file exists with ls - ls : list files inside a directory
- lh : list them in a human readable form
ls -lh data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt
head -n 5 data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt
This is a tab-delimited text file. Print the header with one field per line to inspect its variable names:
head -n 1 data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt | tr '\t' '\n'






TipThings to understand



What does tr do in the command above?
The | in the command is a called a pipe. What does it do?


Step 3: Explore the data
Count the total lines present in the file, including the header.

wc -l data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt
View the file with cat.
cat data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt
That is too much data to look at. Lets just peek at the header for the file.
head data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt
View the complete file interactively; press q to quit.
less data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt
Search for a known trait, population, family, or other text value.

Replace SEARCH_TERM with a value that occurs in the data.

Lets search for the population ALB in the data set.

grep "SEARCH_TERM" data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt | head






TipCan you find the how many families/individuals are from VT (Vermont) location?



Hint!
1. Break it down into individual steps.
2. Then combine them together with pipes.








NoteWrap Up



Before continuing, identify the data-file header, count the total lines, and write down two variables you expect to be numeric. Do not assume a column’s type from its name alone: check the data.

title: R: Basics for reproducible data analysis
text:
Learn core R syntax and data-handling skills by analyzing the red-spruce fitness-trait dataset you already downloaded in Bashing the cluster, and finish with a first reproducible R script whose outputs land in results/.
This module picks up exactly where the cluster exercise left off: data/raw/ holds the raw file, src/ will hold your R scripts, and results/ will hold everything R produces.




Completed the cluster exercise
R (>= 4.2) installed; RStudio recommended but not required
The dataset available at data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt

If you’re working locally instead of on the cluster, grab the same file directly from R:

dir.create("data/raw", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
download.file(
"https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anoobvinu07/Genomic_assisted_selection/master/data/FitnessTraits_GeneticParameters_RedSpruce.txt",
      destfile = "data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt")

Recreate the rest of the project layout if you don’t already have it:

dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create("src", showWarnings = FALSE)







ImportantProject directory setup





This excercise assumes the project folder follows the following structure:
cluster-exercise/
 ├── data/
 │   └── raw/       # downloaded, unchanged source data
 ├── logs/          # Slurm standard output and error logs
 ├── results/       # analysis products created by R
 └── src/           # R and Slurm scripts

title: R: Basics for reproducible data analysis
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this module you should be able to:

Start R/RStudio with a reproducible working directory (no hard-coded absolute paths)
Describe R’s core data types and structures: vectors, factors, data frames, lists
Import and inspect a tab-delimited file
Subset, filter, and summarize data with base R
Produce basic plots (histogram, boxplot, scatterplot)
Save tables and plots into results/
Turn interactive code into a script you can run non-interactively with Rscript

title: R: Basics for reproducible data analysis
text:
Setting up your R project
On the cluster, load R and start it from inside cluster-exercise/:

cd ~/projects/cluster-exercise

module biocontainers/default
module load r          # module name may differ on your cluster; check `module avail r`

R                      # start the R session

Inside R, always confirm where you are before reading or writing anything:

getwd()

[1] "/Users/anoobprakash/Documents/GitHub/anoobvinu07.github.io/notebook/posts/r-basics"


If you’re using RStudio, create an RStudio Project (File > New Project) rooted at cluster-exercise/ — this keeps every path relative and portable, exactly like the data/raw/... paths from the bash module.

title: R: Basics for reproducible data analysis
text:
R data types and structures

# Vectors: one-dimensional, single type
heights <- c(27.3, 31.1, 29.6, 32.0)
pops    <- c("AB", "AB", "CC", "CC")

# Factors: categorical vectors with fixed levels
region <- factor(c("E", "E", "C", "C"))
levels(region)

[1] "C" "E"

# Data frames: a table — columns can be different types
df_demo <- data.frame(pop = pops, height = heights)
str(df_demo)

'data.frame':   4 obs. of  2 variables:
 $ pop   : chr  "AB" "AB" "CC" "CC"
 $ height: num  27.3 31.1 29.6 32

# Lists: can hold mixed, differently-shaped objects
result <- list(mean_height = mean(heights), populations = unique(pops))
result$mean_height

[1] 30


Key idea: almost everything you do in this module is a data frame — one row per tree, one column per variable — with vectors as its columns.

Importing and inspecting the dataset

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
text: Simulate two populations at a single biallelic gene using sample() and replicate(), calculate genotype and allele frequencies for each, then combine them into one table to explore how those frequencies shift with population size and starting allele frequency.

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
text: Simulate two populations at a single biallelic gene using sample() and replicate(), calculate genotype and allele frequencies for each, then combine them into one table to explore how those frequencies shift with population size and starting allele frequency.

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
text:
Prerequisites

Completed Modules 1–2 (functions, if/else, for loops, table(), grouped summaries)
No external dataset needed — this module is entirely simulation-based

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this module you should be able to:

Use sample() to draw alleles for an individual under a given allele frequency
Use replicate() to generate genotypes for many individuals, and for many simulated populations
Calculate genotype frequencies (AA, Aa, aa) and allele frequencies (A, a) from simulated data
Explain the difference between rbind()/bind_rows() (stacking rows) and merge()/*_join() (matching rows by a shared key), and pick the right one for combining populations
Combine two or more simulated populations into a single data frame and compute frequencies per population
Observe how sampling variance in allele frequency depends on population size — a first hands-on look at genetic drift

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
text:
R quick reference








Function
Purpose
Example




sample()
Draw random values, with weights via prob
sample(c("A","a"), 2, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.6, 0.4))


replicate()
Repeat an expression n times
replicate(50, simulate_genotype(0.6))


table()
Tally counts
table(genotypes)


prop.table()
Convert counts to proportions
prop.table(table(genotypes))


factor(x, levels=...)
Fix category order, including zero-count categories
factor(g, levels = c("AA","Aa","aa"))


rbind()
Stack rows of two same-column data frames
rbind(pop1, pop2)


merge() / dplyr::*_join()
Match rows by a shared key column
merge(df1, df2, by = "id")


tapply() / by()
Apply a function within groups
tapply(combined$genotype, combined$population, table)


do.call(rbind, list)
Stack many data frames from a list at once
do.call(rbind, results_list)


boxplot()
Compare distributions across groups
boxplot(freq_A ~ size, data = df)

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
section: Section 2: One population, many individuals — replicate()
text:
Section 2: One population, many individuals — replicate()
replicate() repeats an expression a fixed number of times and collects the results — exactly what you need to generate genotypes for many individuals:
simulate_population <- function(n, p) {
  genotypes <- replicate(n, simulate_genotype(p))
  data.frame(individual = seq_len(n), genotype = genotypes, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}

pop_demo <- simulate_population(n = 20, p = 0.5)
head(pop_demo)

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
text:
Section 3: Genotype frequencies
geno_counts <- table(factor(pop_demo$genotype, levels = c("AA", "Aa", "aa")))
geno_freq   <- prop.table(geno_counts)
geno_freq
Wrapping the genotype column in factor(..., levels = c("AA","Aa","aa")) guarantees all three categories show up — including with a count of zero — instead of silently dropping a genotype that happened not to appear.
Compare this to the Hardy-Weinberg expectation for allele frequency p:
hwe_expected <- function(p) {
  q <- 1 - p
  c(AA = p^2, Aa = 2 * p * q, aa = q^2)
}
hwe_expected(0.5)

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
text:
Section 4: Allele frequencies from genotypes
Break each genotype string back into its two alleles and tally them:
allele_freq <- function(genotype_vec) {
  alleles <- unlist(strsplit(genotype_vec, ""))
  prop.table(table(alleles))
}

allele_freq(pop_demo$genotype)
The two allele frequencies should sum to 1 — a quick sanity check worth building into any script.

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
section: Section 5: Two populations, and combining them with rbind()
text:
Section 5: Two populations, and combining them with rbind()
pop1 <- simulate_population(n = 40, p = 0.7)
pop1$population <- "Pop1"

pop2 <- simulate_population(n = 15, p = 0.3)
pop2$population <- "Pop2"

combined <- rbind(pop1, pop2)
combined <- combined[, c("population", "individual", "genotype")]

table(combined$population)   # should read Pop1 = 40, Pop2 = 15

rbind() vs. join(): which one do you need?

rbind() (base R) or dplyr::bind_rows() — stack rows from two objects that already share the same columns. This is how you combine two independently simulated populations into one long table, which is exactly what “adding populations together” means here.
merge() (base R) or dplyr::*_join() (left_join(), inner_join(), etc.) — match rows across two tables by a shared key column (e.g., attaching environmental data to individuals by an ID). This solves a different problem and is not what you want for stacking two simulated populations.

For this exercise, rbind() is the right tool.

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
text:
Section 6: Per-population frequency comparison
genotype_freq_by_pop <- tapply(
  combined$genotype, combined$population,
  function(g) prop.table(table(factor(g, levels = c("AA", "Aa", "aa"))))
)
genotype_freq_by_pop

allele_freq_by_pop <- tapply(combined$genotype, combined$population, allele_freq)
allele_freq_by_pop

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
section: Section 7: Exploring the effect of population size (genetic drift)
text:
Section 7: Exploring the effect of population size (genetic drift)
Simulate populations of different sizes at the same true allele frequency, many times over, and look at how much the simulated allele frequency bounces around:
sizes  <- c(5, 20, 50, 200)
p_true <- 0.5
n_reps <- 100

drift_list <- lapply(sizes, function(n) {
  freqs <- replicate(n_reps, {
    pop <- simulate_population(n, p_true)
    af  <- allele_freq(pop$genotype)
    unname(af["A"])
  })
  data.frame(size = n, replicate = seq_len(n_reps), freq_A = freqs)
})

drift_df <- do.call(rbind, drift_list)

aggregate(freq_A ~ size, data = drift_df, FUN = sd)

boxplot(freq_A ~ size, data = drift_df,
        xlab = "Population size", ylab = "Simulated allele frequency (A)",
        main = "Sampling variance shrinks as population size grows")
abline(h = p_true, col = "red", lty = 2)
Smaller populations show a much wider spread of simulated allele frequencies around the true value (the red dashed line) than larger ones — this is genetic drift in its simplest form: random sampling of gametes causes allele frequencies to bounce around more when fewer individuals are sampled each generation.

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
section: Section 8: Exploring the effect of starting allele frequency
text:
Section 8: Exploring the effect of starting allele frequency
Hold population size fixed and vary p instead, comparing observed genotype frequencies to the Hardy-Weinberg expectation:
p_values <- c(0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9)
n_fixed  <- 50

geno_freq_list <- lapply(p_values, function(p) {
  pop <- simulate_population(n_fixed, p)
  observed <- prop.table(table(factor(pop$genotype, levels = c("AA", "Aa", "aa"))))
  expected <- hwe_expected(p)
  data.frame(p = p, genotype = names(observed),
             observed = as.numeric(observed),
             expected = as.numeric(expected[names(observed)]))
})

geno_freq_df <- do.call(rbind, geno_freq_list)
geno_freq_df
Notice that Aa (heterozygote) frequency peaks at intermediate p, exactly as 2pq predicts.

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
text:
Idea check
Work through these before the exercises.

Why does simulate_genotype() draw with replace = TRUE instead of replace = FALSE?
What goes wrong if you tally genotypes by pasting the two sampled alleles directly (paste(alleles, collapse = "")) instead of counting copies of A? How does simulate_genotype() avoid that problem?
What is the practical difference between rbind() and a join() such as merge() or dplyr::left_join()? Why is rbind() the correct choice for combining two independently simulated populations?
Under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium with allele frequency p, what are the expected genotype frequencies for AA, Aa, and aa? At what value of p is the heterozygote frequency (Aa) maximized?
If you simulate a population of size 10 versus size 500 at the same true p, what do you expect to happen to the spread of the resulting allele-frequency estimates across many replicate simulations — and why?
Why is factor(genotype, levels = c("AA","Aa","aa")) used before calling table(), rather than just calling table(genotype) directly?
Why might a small, isolated real forest population show allele frequencies that drift further from an “expected” value than a large, well-connected population?

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
text:
Practical exercises

Write simulate_genotype(p) and generate a genotype for one individual at p = 0.5 ten separate times. Confirm you see a mix of AA, Aa, and aa.
Write simulate_population(n, p) using replicate() and generate a population of n = 50 individuals at p = 0.5.
Calculate genotype frequencies for this population with table()/prop.table(), and compare them to hwe_expected(0.5).
Write allele_freq() and calculate allele frequencies for the same population. Confirm the two frequencies sum to 1.
Simulate a second population with a size and allele frequency of your choosing (different from step 2), and calculate its genotype and allele frequencies.
Combine both populations into a single data frame using rbind(). Confirm the combined data frame has the expected total number of rows and a population column identifying each row’s origin.
Use tapply() (or by()) on the combined data frame to calculate genotype and allele frequencies separately per population, and confirm the results match what you got individually in steps 3–5.
Run the population-size drift experiment from Section 7 using sizes c(5, 20, 50, 200), p_true = 0.5, and n_reps = 100. Produce the boxplot and describe the pattern in one sentence.
Run the allele-frequency experiment from Section 8 using p_values <- c(0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9) at n = 50. Confirm your observed Aa frequencies roughly track 2pq across the range of p.
Save every table you produced (genotype frequencies, allele frequencies, the drift summary, the observed-vs-expected table) to results/, and the boxplot as a PNG.

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
text:
Homework (weeks 1–2)
Build a self-contained src/03_simulate_populations.R that:

Defines reusable simulate_genotype(), simulate_population(), allele_freq(), and hwe_expected() functions.
Simulates at least 3 populations with different combinations of size and starting allele frequency, and combines them with rbind() into one data frame.
Computes and saves a clean per-population summary table of genotype and allele frequencies to results/.
Runs a drift experiment (as in Section 7) with at least 4 population sizes and at least 50 replicates each at a fixed p, and saves the boxplot of allele-frequency spread by size to results/.
Includes a written interpretation (half a page, as script comments or results/README.md) answering:

How does population size affect how far a single simulated population’s allele frequency can drift from the true p?
Connect this pattern to a real scenario in forest genetics — for example, small, fragmented, or edge-of-range tree populations versus large, continuous ones.


Bonus (optional): extend the simulation across non-overlapping generations — each generation, resample the next generation’s alleles from the previous generation’s genotype pool instead of from a fixed p. This is a minimal Wright-Fisher drift simulation and is a natural bridge toward the coalescent- and drift-aware methods used in genomic-offset validation work.
Submission format: src/03_simulate_populations.R, everything it generates in results/, and the written interpretation.
Suggested pace: 2–3 hours per week over 1–2 weeks.

Genotypes at a biallelic SNP are usually coded as the count of the alternate allele: 0 (homozygous reference), 1 (heterozygous), 2 (homozygous alternate). Let’s simulate a toy dataset — 30 individuals, 10 loci:

set.seed(123)
n_ind  <- 30 # number of individuals
n_loci <- 10 # number of SNP loci

This code creates a simulated genotype matrix where rows are individuals, columns are SNP loci, and each cell contains a diploid genotype coded as 0, 1, or 2.

geno <- matrix(
  sample(0:2,                # sample values from 0, 1 or 2
  n_ind * n_loci,            # no. of draws 30 x 10 or size of the matrix
  replace = TRUE,            # each genotype category can be drawn repeatedly
  prob = c(0.4, 0.4, 0.2)),  # sampling probability for genotypes 0,1 and 2
  nrow = n_ind,              # number of rows - filled with ind IDs
  ncol = n_loci              # number of columns - filled with SNP IDs
)







NoteLogic check






Genotype codingGenotype probability


For a biallelic SNP, the number represents the count of the alternate allele carried by an individual:



Value
Genotypes
Biological meaning




0
0/0
Homozygous reference; zero alternate alleles


1
0/1
Heterozygous; one alternate allele


2
1/1
Homozygous alternate; two alternate alleles



So, for example, a 1 in row ind_7 and column locus_3 means individual 7 is heterozygous at SNP locus 3.

title: R for Bioinformatics: Population Genetics Foundations
section: A minimal SNP genotype matrix in R
text:
A minimal SNP genotype matrix in R
Genotypes at a biallelic SNP are usually coded as the count of the alternate allele: 0 (homozygous reference), 1 (heterozygous), 2 (homozygous alternate). Let’s simulate a toy dataset — 30 individuals, 10 loci:

set.seed(123)
n_ind  <- 30
n_loci <- 10

geno <- matrix(
  sample(0:2, n_ind * n_loci, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.4, 0.4, 0.2)),
  nrow = n_ind, ncol = n_loci
)
rownames(geno) <- paste0("ind_", 1:n_ind)
colnames(geno) <- paste0("locus_", 1:n_loci)

geno[1:5, 1:5]

      locus_1 locus_2 locus_3 locus_4 locus_5
ind_1       1       2       0       1       0
ind_2       0       2       1       0       1
ind_3       0       0       1       1       1
ind_4       2       0       1       0       1
ind_5       2       1       2       1       1

title: R for Bioinformatics: Population Genetics Foundations
text:
Allele frequencies
Each genotype value is the count of the alternate allele out of 2, so the mean genotype divided by 2 is the alternate allele frequency for that locus:

alt_freq <- colMeans(geno) / 2
ref_freq <- 1 - alt_freq

data.frame(locus = names(alt_freq), alt_freq = round(alt_freq, 3), ref_freq = round(ref_freq, 3))

            locus alt_freq ref_freq
locus_1   locus_1    0.400    0.600
locus_2   locus_2    0.383    0.617
locus_3   locus_3    0.383    0.617
locus_4   locus_4    0.367    0.633
locus_5   locus_5    0.400    0.600

locus_7   locus_7    0.417    0.583

locus_9   locus_9    0.367    0.633
locus_10 locus_10    0.450    0.550

title: R for Bioinformatics: Population Genetics Foundations
text:
Observed and expected heterozygosity
Observed heterozygosity (Ho): the proportion of individuals with genotype 1 (heterozygous) at a locus.
Expected heterozygosity (He): what you’d expect under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, given the allele frequencies: (He = 2pq), where (p) and (q) are the reference and alternate allele frequencies.

Ho <- colMeans(geno == 1)
He <- 2 * ref_freq * alt_freq

het_table <- data.frame(locus = names(Ho), Ho = round(Ho, 3), He = round(He, 3),
                         diff = round(Ho - He, 3))
het_table

            locus    Ho    He   diff
locus_1   locus_1 0.267 0.480 -0.213
locus_2   locus_2 0.500 0.473  0.027
locus_3   locus_3 0.367 0.473 -0.106
locus_4   locus_4 0.333 0.464 -0.131
locus_5   locus_5 0.467 0.480 -0.013
locus_6   locus_6 0.433 0.433  0.001
locus_7   locus_7 0.367 0.486 -0.119
locus_8   locus_8 0.400 0.480 -0.080
locus_9   locus_9 0.333 0.464 -0.131
locus_10 locus_10 0.567 0.495  0.072


If Ho is consistently lower than He across loci, that’s a signature of inbreeding or population substructure — the same underlying idea behind the Family_Homozygosity and Population_Homozygosity columns already computed in your real dataset.

title: R for Bioinformatics: Population Genetics Foundations
text:
PCA for population structure
On the simulated matrix:

pca_sim <- prcomp(geno, scale. = TRUE)
plot(pca_sim$x[, 1], pca_sim$x[, 2],
     xlab = "PC1", ylab = "PC2", main = "Simulated genotype PCA")








Now look at the real PC1/PC2 already computed for the red-spruce trees (from actual genetic markers, not simulated):

traits <- read.table("data/raw/red_spruce_fitness_traits.txt", header = TRUE, sep = "\t")


traits$Region <- factor(traits$Region)
plot(traits$PC1, traits$PC2,
     col = as.integer(traits$Region), pch = 19,
     xlab = "PC1", ylab = "PC2", main = "Genetic PCA colored by region")
legend("topright", legend = levels(traits$Region),
       col = 1:nlevels(traits$Region), pch = 19)








In population genetics, PC1/PC2 from a genetic marker PCA usually capture the strongest axes of population structure — often correlated with geography (isolation by distance) or major environmental gradients.

title: R for Bioinformatics: Population Genetics Foundations
text:
A simple genotype/phenotype–environment association
Real GEA work asks: does a genetic or fitness metric covary with an environmental gradient? Start simple, with one predictor at a time:

cor.test(traits$Population_Homozygosity, traits$Elevation)


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  traits$Population_Homozygosity and traits$Elevation
t = 0.84647, df = 321, p-value = 0.3979
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.06225666  0.15552098
sample estimates:
       cor 
0.04719295 

cor.test(traits$Genetic_Diversity, traits$Latitude)


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  traits$Genetic_Diversity and traits$Latitude
t = 5.0142, df = 324, p-value = 8.786e-07
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.1645205 0.3662974
sample estimates:
      cor 
0.2683498 


Then extend to multiple predictors with a linear model:

fit <- lm(Genetic_Load ~ Elevation + Latitude, data = traits)
summary(fit)


Call:
lm(formula = Genetic_Load ~ Elevation + Latitude, data = traits)

Residuals:
       Min         1Q     Median         3Q        Max 
-0.0163979 -0.0062761 -0.0003671  0.0042973  0.0243703 

Coefficients:
              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  1.007e+00  1.138e-02  88.486   <2e-16 ***
Elevation   -4.631e-06  1.882e-06  -2.461   0.0144 *

---

  (3 observations deleted due to missingness)

title: R for Bioinformatics: Population Genetics Foundations
section: From a single correlation to RDA
text:
From a single correlation to RDA
A correlation or lm() only handles one response variable at a time. When you have several genetic/fitness variables you want to relate to several environmental variables together, redundancy analysis (RDA) is the standard multivariate approach in landscape genomics:

library(vegan)

Loading required package: permute

response_vars <- traits[, c("Genetic_Diversity", "Genetic_Load", "PC1", "PC2")]
env_vars <- traits[, c("Elevation", "Latitude")]

rda_fit <- rda(response_vars ~ Elevation + Latitude, data = env_vars, na.action = na.omit)
summary(rda_fit)


Call:
rda(formula = response_vars ~ Elevation + Latitude, data = env_vars,      na.action = na.omit) 

Partitioning of variance:
               Inertia Proportion
Total         0.005753     1.0000
Constrained   0.002715     0.4719
Unconstrained 0.003038     0.5281

Eigenvalues, and their contribution to the variance 

Importance of components:
                          RDA1      RDA2     PC1       PC2       PC3       PC4
Eigenvalue            0.002312 0.0004031 0.00233 0.0005979 7.385e-05 3.614e-05
Proportion Explained  0.401805 0.0700740 0.40507 0.1039361 1.284e-02 6.282e-03
Cumulative Proportion 0.401805 0.4718786 0.87694 0.9808800 9.937e-01 1.000e+00

Accumulated constrained eigenvalues
Importance of components:
                          RDA1      RDA2
Eigenvalue            0.002312 0.0004031
Proportion Explained  0.851500 0.1485001
Cumulative Proportion 0.851500 1.0000000

plot(rda_fit)








This is a simplified stand-in for the genotype-environment association / genomic-offset workflows you’d run on real SNP data (e.g., with LEA, gradientForest, or full-genotype RDA) — the mechanics of centering the response, fitting the constrained ordination, and reading the biplot are the same.

title: R for Bioinformatics: Population Genetics Foundations
text:
Roadmap beyond this module
When you’re ready to work with real genotype data instead of pre-computed summaries:

vcfR::read.vcfR() reads a VCF file into R
adegenet::df2genind() / vcfR::vcfR2genind() convert genotypes into population-genetics-aware objects with built-in allele-frequency, heterozygosity, and Fst functions
LEA (Bioconductor) and vegan::rda() scale the GEA approach above to genome-wide SNP data

None of this is required for this module’s exercises — it’s here so you know where basics you learn connects to your actual genomic analysis pipelines.

title: R for Bioinformatics: Population Genetics Foundations
text:
Idea check
Answer these before the practical exercises.

What does an alternate allele frequency of 0.3 at a locus mean biologically?
Why can observed heterozygosity (Ho) be lower than expected heterozygosity (He) in a real population?
What do you think Population_Homozygosity is measuring, and how would you expect it to relate to Genetic_Diversity — positively or negatively?
In a PCA built from genetic markers, what do PC1 and PC2 typically represent in a population-genetics context?
Why test cor.test(Genetic_Diversity, Elevation) rather than just assuming a relationship exists because both vary by population?
What is the conceptual difference between running a separate lm() for each genetic variable versus running one rda() with all of them as a response matrix?

title: R for Bioinformatics: Population Genetics Foundations
text:
Practical exercises

Build the simulated genotype matrix (30 individuals × 10 loci) exactly as shown, and compute the alternate allele frequency for every locus.
Compute observed and expected heterozygosity for each locus and identify which locus shows the largest Ho − He gap.
Run prcomp() on the simulated genotype matrix and plot PC1 vs. PC2.
Load the real red-spruce dataset and plot the real PC1 vs. PC2, colored by Region. Does the pattern look like discrete clusters or a continuous gradient?
Run cor.test() between Population_Homozygosity and Elevation, and separately between Genetic_Diversity and Latitude. Report the correlation coefficient, p-value, and a one-sentence interpretation for each.
Fit lm(Genetic_Load ~ Elevation + Latitude, data = traits) and interpret the two coefficients — which predictor has a stronger association, and in which direction?
Stretch exercise: run the vegan::rda() example above using Genetic_Diversity, Genetic_Load, PC1, PC2 as responses and Elevation, Latitude as predictors. Produce the ordination biplot and describe what you see in 2–3 sentences.
Save every summary table (allele frequencies, heterozygosity table, correlation results) and every plot into results/.

title: R for Bioinformatics: Population Genetics Foundations
text:
Homework (weeks 1–2)
Build src/02_pop_genetics_intro.R, combining the simulated-data fundamentals with a real-data GEA-style analysis.
Requirements:

Part A (fundamentals): allele frequency and Ho/He table for the simulated genotype matrix, plus the PCA plot.
Part B (applied): using the real dataset, test associations between at least two genetic-parameter columns (e.g., Population_Homozygosity, Genetic_Diversity, Genetic_Load) and at least two environmental predictors (Elevation, Latitude, Longitude), using correlation and/or lm().
A written interpretation (half a page, as comments or a results/README.md) answering: Do the genetic parameters show a spatial pattern with latitude or elevation? What ecological or demographic process might explain this (e.g., isolation by distance, local adaptation, drift in small/marginal populations)?
Bonus (optional): complete the vegan::rda() ordination and include the biplot with a short interpretation of which environmental axis drives more separation among genetic variables.

Submission format: src/02_pop_genetics_intro.R, all generated outputs in results/, and the written interpretation.
Suggested pace: 2–3 hours per week over 1–2 weeks, building directly on the Module 1 script and dataset.

Wrap Up

Idea check
Answer these before the practical exercises.

What does an alternate allele frequency of 0.3 at a locus mean biologically?
Why can observed heterozygosity (Ho) be lower than expected heterozygosity (He) in a real population?
What do you think Population_Homozygosity is measuring, and how would you expect it to relate to Genetic_Diversity — positively or negatively?
In a PCA built from genetic markers, what do PC1 and PC2 typically represent in a population-genetics context?
Why test cor.test(Genetic_Diversity, Elevation) rather than just assuming a relationship exists because both vary by population?
What is the conceptual difference between running a separate lm() for each genetic variable versus running one rda() with all of them as a response matrix?



Practical exercises

Build the simulated genotype matrix (30 individuals × 10 loci) exactly as shown, and compute the alternate allele frequency for every locus.
Compute observed and expected heterozygosity for each locus and identify which locus shows the largest Ho − He gap.

Stretch exercise: run the vegan::rda() example above using Genetic_Diversity, Genetic_Load, PC1, PC2 as responses and Elevation, Latitude as predictors. Produce the ordination biplot and describe what you see in 2–3 sentences.
Save every summary table (allele frequencies, heterozygosity table, correlation results) and every plot into results/.

Build src/02_pop_genetics_intro.R, combining the simulated-data fundamentals with a real-data GEA-style analysis.

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
text:
Prerequisites

Completed Modules 1–2 (functions, if/else, for loops, table(), grouped summaries)
No external dataset needed — this module is entirely simulation-based

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this module you should be able to:

Use sample() to draw alleles for an individual under a given allele frequency
Use replicate() to generate genotypes for many individuals, and for many simulated populations
Calculate genotype frequencies (AA, Aa, aa) and allele frequencies (A, a) from simulated data
Explain the difference between rbind()/bind_rows() (stacking rows) and merge()/*_join() (matching rows by a shared key), and pick the right one for combining populations
Combine two or more simulated populations into a single data frame and compute frequencies per population
Observe how sampling variance in allele frequency depends on population size — a first hands-on look at genetic drift

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
text:
R quick reference








Function
Purpose
Example




sample()
Draw random values, with weights via prob
sample(c("A","a"), 2, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.6, 0.4))


replicate()
Repeat an expression n times
replicate(50, simulate_genotype(0.6))


table()
Tally counts
table(genotypes)


prop.table()
Convert counts to proportions
prop.table(table(genotypes))


factor(x, levels=...)
Fix category order, including zero-count categories
factor(g, levels = c("AA","Aa","aa"))


rbind()
Stack rows of two same-column data frames
rbind(pop1, pop2)


merge() / dplyr::*_join()
Match rows by a shared key column
merge(df1, df2, by = "id")


tapply() / by()
Apply a function within groups
tapply(combined$genotype, combined$population, table)


do.call(rbind, list)
Stack many data frames from a list at once
do.call(rbind, results_list)


boxplot()
Compare distributions across groups
boxplot(freq_A ~ size, data = df)

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
section: Section 2: One population, many individuals — replicate()
text:
Section 2: One population, many individuals — replicate()
replicate() repeats an expression a fixed number of times and collects the results — exactly what you need to generate genotypes for many individuals:
simulate_population <- function(n, p) {
  genotypes <- replicate(n, simulate_genotype(p))
  data.frame(individual = seq_len(n), genotype = genotypes, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}

pop_demo <- simulate_population(n = 20, p = 0.5)
head(pop_demo)

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
text:
Section 3: Genotype frequencies
geno_counts <- table(factor(pop_demo$genotype, levels = c("AA", "Aa", "aa")))
geno_freq   <- prop.table(geno_counts)
geno_freq
Wrapping the genotype column in factor(..., levels = c("AA","Aa","aa")) guarantees all three categories show up — including with a count of zero — instead of silently dropping a genotype that happened not to appear.
Compare this to the Hardy-Weinberg expectation for allele frequency p:
hwe_expected <- function(p) {
  q <- 1 - p
  c(AA = p^2, Aa = 2 * p * q, aa = q^2)
}
hwe_expected(0.5)

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
text:
Section 4: Allele frequencies from genotypes
Break each genotype string back into its two alleles and tally them:
allele_freq <- function(genotype_vec) {
  alleles <- unlist(strsplit(genotype_vec, ""))
  prop.table(table(alleles))
}

allele_freq(pop_demo$genotype)
The two allele frequencies should sum to 1 — a quick sanity check worth building into any script.

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
section: Section 5: Two populations, and combining them with rbind()
text:
Section 5: Two populations, and combining them with rbind()
pop1 <- simulate_population(n = 40, p = 0.7)
pop1$population <- "Pop1"

pop2 <- simulate_population(n = 15, p = 0.3)
pop2$population <- "Pop2"

combined <- rbind(pop1, pop2)
combined <- combined[, c("population", "individual", "genotype")]

table(combined$population)   # should read Pop1 = 40, Pop2 = 15

rbind() vs. join(): which one do you need?

rbind() (base R) or dplyr::bind_rows() — stack rows from two objects that already share the same columns. This is how you combine two independently simulated populations into one long table, which is exactly what “adding populations together” means here.
merge() (base R) or dplyr::*_join() (left_join(), inner_join(), etc.) — match rows across two tables by a shared key column (e.g., attaching environmental data to individuals by an ID). This solves a different problem and is not what you want for stacking two simulated populations.

For this exercise, rbind() is the right tool.

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
text:
Section 6: Per-population frequency comparison
genotype_freq_by_pop <- tapply(
  combined$genotype, combined$population,
  function(g) prop.table(table(factor(g, levels = c("AA", "Aa", "aa"))))
)
genotype_freq_by_pop

allele_freq_by_pop <- tapply(combined$genotype, combined$population, allele_freq)
allele_freq_by_pop

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
section: Section 7: Exploring the effect of population size (genetic drift)
text:
Section 7: Exploring the effect of population size (genetic drift)
Simulate populations of different sizes at the same true allele frequency, many times over, and look at how much the simulated allele frequency bounces around:
sizes  <- c(5, 20, 50, 200)
p_true <- 0.5
n_reps <- 100

drift_list <- lapply(sizes, function(n) {
  freqs <- replicate(n_reps, {
    pop <- simulate_population(n, p_true)
    af  <- allele_freq(pop$genotype)
    unname(af["A"])
  })
  data.frame(size = n, replicate = seq_len(n_reps), freq_A = freqs)
})

drift_df <- do.call(rbind, drift_list)

aggregate(freq_A ~ size, data = drift_df, FUN = sd)

boxplot(freq_A ~ size, data = drift_df,
        xlab = "Population size", ylab = "Simulated allele frequency (A)",
        main = "Sampling variance shrinks as population size grows")
abline(h = p_true, col = "red", lty = 2)
Smaller populations show a much wider spread of simulated allele frequencies around the true value (the red dashed line) than larger ones — this is genetic drift in its simplest form: random sampling of gametes causes allele frequencies to bounce around more when fewer individuals are sampled each generation.

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
section: Section 8: Exploring the effect of starting allele frequency
text:
Section 8: Exploring the effect of starting allele frequency
Hold population size fixed and vary p instead, comparing observed genotype frequencies to the Hardy-Weinberg expectation:
p_values <- c(0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9)
n_fixed  <- 50

geno_freq_list <- lapply(p_values, function(p) {
  pop <- simulate_population(n_fixed, p)
  observed <- prop.table(table(factor(pop$genotype, levels = c("AA", "Aa", "aa"))))
  expected <- hwe_expected(p)
  data.frame(p = p, genotype = names(observed),
             observed = as.numeric(observed),
             expected = as.numeric(expected[names(observed)]))
})

geno_freq_df <- do.call(rbind, geno_freq_list)
geno_freq_df
Notice that Aa (heterozygote) frequency peaks at intermediate p, exactly as 2pq predicts.

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
text:
Idea check
Work through these before the exercises.

Why does simulate_genotype() draw with replace = TRUE instead of replace = FALSE?
What goes wrong if you tally genotypes by pasting the two sampled alleles directly (paste(alleles, collapse = "")) instead of counting copies of A? How does simulate_genotype() avoid that problem?
What is the practical difference between rbind() and a join() such as merge() or dplyr::left_join()? Why is rbind() the correct choice for combining two independently simulated populations?
Under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium with allele frequency p, what are the expected genotype frequencies for AA, Aa, and aa? At what value of p is the heterozygote frequency (Aa) maximized?
If you simulate a population of size 10 versus size 500 at the same true p, what do you expect to happen to the spread of the resulting allele-frequency estimates across many replicate simulations — and why?
Why is factor(genotype, levels = c("AA","Aa","aa")) used before calling table(), rather than just calling table(genotype) directly?
Why might a small, isolated real forest population show allele frequencies that drift further from an “expected” value than a large, well-connected population?

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
text:
Practical exercises

Write simulate_genotype(p) and generate a genotype for one individual at p = 0.5 ten separate times. Confirm you see a mix of AA, Aa, and aa.
Write simulate_population(n, p) using replicate() and generate a population of n = 50 individuals at p = 0.5.
Calculate genotype frequencies for this population with table()/prop.table(), and compare them to hwe_expected(0.5).
Write allele_freq() and calculate allele frequencies for the same population. Confirm the two frequencies sum to 1.
Simulate a second population with a size and allele frequency of your choosing (different from step 2), and calculate its genotype and allele frequencies.
Combine both populations into a single data frame using rbind(). Confirm the combined data frame has the expected total number of rows and a population column identifying each row’s origin.
Use tapply() (or by()) on the combined data frame to calculate genotype and allele frequencies separately per population, and confirm the results match what you got individually in steps 3–5.
Run the population-size drift experiment from Section 7 using sizes c(5, 20, 50, 200), p_true = 0.5, and n_reps = 100. Produce the boxplot and describe the pattern in one sentence.
Run the allele-frequency experiment from Section 8 using p_values <- c(0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9) at n = 50. Confirm your observed Aa frequencies roughly track 2pq across the range of p.
Save every table you produced (genotype frequencies, allele frequencies, the drift summary, the observed-vs-expected table) to results/, and the boxplot as a PNG.

title: Simulating Populations: Allele and Genotype Frequencies
text:
Homework (weeks 1–2)
Build a self-contained src/03_simulate_populations.R that:

Defines reusable simulate_genotype(), simulate_population(), allele_freq(), and hwe_expected() functions.
Simulates at least 3 populations with different combinations of size and starting allele frequency, and combines them with rbind() into one data frame.
Computes and saves a clean per-population summary table of genotype and allele frequencies to results/.
Runs a drift experiment (as in Section 7) with at least 4 population sizes and at least 50 replicates each at a fixed p, and saves the boxplot of allele-frequency spread by size to results/.
Includes a written interpretation (half a page, as script comments or results/README.md) answering:

How does population size affect how far a single simulated population’s allele frequency can drift from the true p?
Connect this pattern to a real scenario in forest genetics — for example, small, fragmented, or edge-of-range tree populations versus large, continuous ones.


Bonus (optional): extend the simulation across non-overlapping generations — each generation, resample the next generation’s alleles from the previous generation’s genotype pool instead of from a fixed p. This is a minimal Wright-Fisher drift simulation and is a natural bridge toward the coalescent- and drift-aware methods used in genomic-offset validation work.
Submission format: src/03_simulate_populations.R, everything it generates in results/, and the written interpretation.
Suggested pace: 2–3 hours per week over 1–2 weeks.
