The expected aa count is less than 1 individual. This is why formal goodness-of-fit tests (like chisq.test()) are unreliable here: the standard rule of thumb requires expected counts of at least ~5 per category. With \(q^2 = 0.04\) and N = 20, you would need roughly \(5 / 0.04 = 125\) individuals just to expect 5 aa individuals. Rare genotype classes need large samples.

title: R: Population Genetics Foundations
text:
Excercises

Exercise 1 — Allele frequencies for Population 2
Estimate the allele frequencies \(p_A\) and \(q_a\) for Population 2, following the same steps used for Population 1: count genotypes, count allele copies, and divide by \(2N\). Verify that \(p + q = 1\).






TipSolution






counts_2 <- geno_count_pop2
N_2 <- nrow(pop_2)

n_A_2 <- 2 * counts_2["AA"] + counts_2["Aa"]
n_a_2 <- 2 * counts_2["aa"] + counts_2["Aa"]

p_A_2 <- unname(as.numeric(n_A_2 / (2 * N_2)))
q_a_2 <- unname(as.numeric(n_a_2 / (2 * N_2)))

p_A_2

[1] 0.35

q_a_2

[1] 0.65

p_A_2 + q_a_2

[1] 1


With set.seed(42), Population 2 has 2 AA, 10 Aa, 8 aa, so:
\[p_{A} = \frac{(2 \times 2) + 10}{40} = \frac{14}{40} = 0.35\]
\[q_{a} = \frac{(2 \times 8) + 10}{40} = \frac{26}{40} = 0.65\]
Again the observed \(p\) (0.35) sits above the simulation input (0.30) — finite-sample noise. The two populations are strongly differentiated at this locus: \(p_A\) = 0.70 vs. 0.35.





Exercise 2 — Allele frequencies for the pooled population
Compute the allele frequencies for the pooled population (Pop_1 + Pop_2). Compare them to the within-population values, and explain the pattern: where does the pooled estimate fall, and why?






TipSolution






counts_p <- geno_count_pooled
N_p <- nrow(pooled_population)

n_A_p <- 2 * counts_p["AA"] + counts_p["Aa"]
n_a_p <- 2 * counts_p["aa"] + counts_p["Aa"]

p_A_p <- unname(as.numeric(n_A_p / (2 * N_p)))
q_a_p <- unname(as.numeric(n_a_p / (2 * N_p)))

p_A_p

[1] 0.525

q_a_p

[1] 0.475


Pooled counts are 11 AA, 20 Aa, 9 aa (40 individuals, 80 gene copies):
\[p_{A} = \frac{(2 \times 11) + 20}{80} = \frac{42}{80} = 0.525\]
\[q_{a} = \frac{(2 \times 9) + 20}{80} = \frac{38}{80} = 0.475\]
The pooled \(p_A\) = 0.525 is almost exactly the average of the two within-population frequencies:
\[\frac{p_{A,1} + p_{A,2}}{2} = \frac{0.70 + 0.35}{2} = 0.525\]
(With unequal population sizes, the pooled frequency is a weighted average, weighted by each population’s size.) Mixing does not create or destroy alleles — it just averages them. But as the next exercise shows, it does distort genotype frequencies.





Exercise 3 — Pooling changes genotype frequencies
Using the geno_summary table you built earlier:

Compute the expected genotype frequencies for the pooled population from its allele frequencies (\(p^2\), \(2pq\), \(q^2\)).
Compare them to the observed pooled genotype frequencies.
Compute the expected genotype frequencies you would get by averaging the two populations’ own H–W expectations.
Which comparison do the observed pooled frequencies resemble more? Why?







TipSolution






# 1. H-W expectations from the POOLED allele frequencies
exp_pooled_from_pool_p <- c(AA = p_A_p^2, Aa = 2 * p_A_p * q_a_p, aa = q_a_p^2)

# 2. Observed pooled genotype frequencies
obs_pooled <- as.numeric(geno_prop_pooled[c("AA", "Aa", "aa")])

# 3. Average of the two populations' OWN H-W expectations
exp_avg_of_pops <- c(
  AA = (p_1^2 + p_2^2) / 2,
  Aa = (2 * p_1 * q_1 + 2 * p_2 * q_2) / 2,
  aa = (q_1^2 + q_2^2) / 2
)

rbind(
  observed            = obs_pooled,
  HW_from_pooled_p    = exp_pooled_from_pool_p,
  avg_of_pop_HW       = exp_avg_of_pops
)

                       AA      Aa       aa
observed         0.275000 0.50000 0.225000
HW_from_pooled_p 0.275625 0.49875 0.225625
avg_of_pop_HW    0.365000 0.37000 0.265000


Using the seed-42 numbers (\(p_{pool} = 0.525\)):

H–W from pooled \(p\): \(AA = 0.276\), \(Aa = 0.499\), \(aa = 0.226\)
Average of the two populations’ own expectations: \(AA = 0.365\), \(Aa = 0.370\), \(aa = 0.265\)

Here is the interesting part: at this seed, the observed pooled frequencies (0.275 / 0.500 / 0.225) land almost exactly on the H–W line from the pooled \(p\) — the Wahlund deficit is invisible. Compare the two reference rows to see why the deficit should be there: H–W from the pooled \(p\) predicts 49.9% heterozygotes, but heterozygotes in the mixture can only come from the two populations’ own heterozygote proportions, which average 37%. The systematic expectation is a 13-point heterozygote deficit — the Wahlund effect.
Why can’t we see it? At \(N = 20\) per population, the standard error of a genotype proportion near 0.5 is about \(\sqrt{0.25/20} \approx 0.11\) — the same size as the deficit itself. In this seed, Pop_1 happened to draw a heterozygote excess (10 observed vs. 6.4 expected), which cancels the Wahlund gap almost perfectly.
The takeaway is not that the effect is fake, but that at small N it is buried in noise. Pooling two H–W populations systematically produces a heterozygote deficit relative to H–W expectations computed from the pooled allele frequencies — no population evolved, only the reference frame changed. Part III re-runs this exact comparison at \(N = 500\) per population, where the deficit stands out unmistakably.





Exercise 4 — Allele frequencies from the genotype matrix
Return to the 30 individuals \(\times\) 10 loci matrix geno from Part I.

Compute the alternate allele frequency for every locus by hand using allele counting (2*n2 + n1 divided by 2*N), not colMeans().
Verify that your result matches colMeans(geno) / 2 exactly.
Compute the minor allele frequency (MAF) for each locus. Which locus is closest to fixation? Which is most variable?







TipSolution






N <- nrow(geno)

# 1. Allele counting, locus by locus
n_alt <- 2 * colSums(geno == 2) + colSums(geno == 1)
alt_freq_manual <- n_alt / (2 * N)

# 2. Cross-check with the shortcut
all.equal(as.numeric(alt_freq_manual), as.numeric(alt_freq))

[1] TRUE

# 3. Minor allele frequency
maf <- pmin(alt_freq, 1 - alt_freq)
sort(round(maf, 3))

 locus_6  locus_4  locus_9  locus_2  locus_3  locus_1  locus_5  locus_8 
   0.317    0.367    0.367    0.383    0.383    0.400    0.400    0.400 
 locus_7 locus_10 
   0.417    0.450 


all.equal() confirms the two computations agree — colMeans(geno)/2 is just algebraically compressed allele counting: the mean of a 0/1/2 column is \((n_{het} + 2 \cdot n_{homAlt}) / N\), which divided by 2 is exactly the alternate allele frequency.
For the MAF, the least variable locus is locus_6 (alt = 0.317, MAF \(\approx\) 0.317) and the most variable is locus_10 (alt = 0.450, MAF \(\approx\) 0.450). The most informative loci for GEA are the ones with MAF near 0.5, which is why filtering pipelines typically drop loci with MAF below 0.05: rare variants carry little signal and inflate noise.





Exercise 5 — Explore the simulation
Change one thing at a time and re-run the whole Part II pipeline. Before you run each variant, write down what you expect to happen; then check.

Sample size: set both populations to size = 500. Do observed frequencies land closer to the H–W expectations?
Similar populations: set \(p_2 = 0.75\). What happens to the pooled genotype frequencies and the Wahlund gap?
Divergent populations: set \(p_2 = 0.05\). What happens?
Different seed: change set.seed(42) to another number. Which quantities change (counts, frequencies) and which relationships stay fixed (\(p + q = 1\), pooled \(p\) = average of within-population \(p\))?







TipSolution — what you should see





Sample size (N = 500): observed genotype frequencies converge on the H–W expectations. Sampling noise shrinks like \(1/\sqrt{N}\) — ten times the sample, about three times less noise. This is the single most reliable way to distinguish “sampling noise” from “real deviation from H–W”.
Similar populations (\(p_2 = 0.75\)): the two populations are nearly indistinguishable at this locus. Pooling barely changes anything — there is almost no Wahlund effect because there is almost no structure. Weak structure = weak heterozygote deficit.
Divergent populations (\(p_2 = 0.05\)): the contrast is extreme — Pop_1 is nearly all AA, Pop_2 nearly all aa. The pooled sample looks like a classic heterozygote-deficient population even though each source population is in perfect H–W equilibrium. Strong structure = strong apparent deficit. This is the situation that most often fools naive analyses of mixed samples (e.g., pooling before computing heterozygosity in a VCF).
Different seed: the counts and frequencies all shift slightly, but the relationships hold: \(p + q = 1\) in every population and the pooled \(p\) always equals the (size-weighted) average of within-population \(p\). Identities survive randomness; estimates don’t.
One practical gotcha when you change seeds or parameters: if a genotype class happens not to occur (e.g., no aa individuals in Pop_1), table() silently drops that level and indexing counts["aa"] returns NA. Keep all three classes with table(factor(pop_1$genotype, levels = c("AA", "Aa", "aa"))) so counts of zero are explicit.

title: R: Population Genetics Foundations
text:
How everything connects
Everything in this module is one pipeline applied at increasing scale. Trace it end-to-end with a single question: “why is this locus heterozygote-deficient?”









Step
Concept
Where you computed it
Red-spruce equivalent




1
Count genotypes
table(pop_1$genotype)
—


2
Allele frequencies \(p, q\)
colMeans(geno)/2, allele counting
—


3
H–W expectations \(p^2, 2pq, q^2\)
prob = c(p^2, 2pq, q^2)
—


4
Observed vs. expected heterozygosity
Ho, He, het_table
Genetic_Diversity


5
The gap: \(F = 1 - H_o/H_e\)
Exercise 7
Family_Homozygosity (conceptually related)


6
Structure causes the gap
Wahlund effect (N = 500 demo)
Region, PC1, PC2


7
Structure detected multivariately
prcomp() PCA plot
PC1, PC2 columns


8
Structure + environment
cor.test(), lm()
Elevation, Latitude


9
Many loci + environment jointly
vegan::rda() (stretch)
RDA / genomic offset



Three threads run through the whole table:

The same two quantities everywhere. Every row is computed from genotype counts and sample size. Heterozygosity, F, the Wahlund effect, PCA loadings, and even the RDA ordination are all functions of allele frequencies — the only thing that changes is how many loci and how many environmental axes you let in.
Structure is the recurring confounder. Pooling populations inflates apparent diversity (Part II, Wahlund), heterozygote deficits can mean either inbreeding or structure (Part III), and the PCA that reveals structure (PC1/PC2) is also the covariate you must control before interpreting any genotype–environment association (Part III’s lm() and rda()). A climate correlation that survives after accounting for structure is evidence of local adaptation; one that disappears was ancestry all along.
Scale changes confidence, not logic. With N = 20 at one locus, noise dominates (Exercise 6). With N = 500, the Wahlund effect is obvious. With 10 loci, averaging helps (Exercise 7). With genome-wide SNPs, per-locus estimates are noise but multivariate summaries (PCA, RDA) become powerful. The math you did by hand on a 2-allele, 20-individual toy is the same math inside adegenet, LEA, and your genomic-offset pipelines.

When you reach the stretch exercise — rda() with Genetic_Diversity, Genetic_Load, PC1, PC2 as responses and Elevation, Latitude as predictors — notice what it is: rows 8 and 9 of the table. A correlation tests one response–predictor pair; the RDA tests all of them jointly, in the same way the PCA summarized all loci jointly. Multivariate = the same idea, more axes.

title: R: Population Genetics Foundations
text:
Roadmap beyond this module
When you’re ready to work with real genotype data instead of pre-computed summaries:

vcfR::read.vcfR() reads a VCF file into R
adegenet::df2genind() / vcfR::vcfR2genind() convert genotypes into population-genetics-aware objects with built-in allele-frequency, heterozygosity, and Fst functions
LEA (Bioconductor) and vegan::rda() scale the GEA approach above to genome-wide SNP data

None of this is required for this module’s exercises — it’s here so you know where basics you learn connects to your actual genomic analysis pipelines.

title: bash: Advanced
text: The guide below is fully interactive: search with //, copy any example, try the redirection visualizer and the quoting playground. For the best experience, open it full screen.

title: bash: Advanced commands to work with Linux systems
text: Every example below has a copy button (top-right of the block). Lines starting with # are comments. Grey-green blocks show what the terminal prints back.

title: bash: Advanced commands to work with Linux systems
text:
Getting oriented
Where you are, what the prompt is telling you, and how to get help without leaving the terminal.

prompt — Read the prompt
The prompt tells you who you are, which machine you are on, and your current directory. On a cluster, the hostname matters: login nodes are shared and are not for heavy computation.


syntax

[user@host directory]$

hostname
login01.cluster.edu
Which node am I on? login01 = shared login node; c0423 = compute node.
whoami
ada
Your username, which is also the owner of your $HOME.
echo $HOME $SCRATCH
/home/ada /scratch/ada
Your home and scratch locations. $SCRATCH is site-specific; check your cluster docs.






Tip



~ at the end of the prompt means you are in your home directory.








Tip



A > prompt instead of $ means the shell is waiting for you to finish something, usually an unclosed quote. Press Ctrl-C to bail out.








Warning



Do not run long or memory-heavy jobs on a login node. Request a compute node with srun --pty bash or submit with sbatch (Slurm).




man / --help — Get help
Every standard command documents itself. --help gives a quick summary; man gives the full manual page.


syntax

man COMMAND   |   COMMAND --help   |   type COMMAND

head --help
Short usage summary for GNU tools.
man wc
Full manual. Space = next page, b = back, /word = search, q = quit.
type cd ls
cd is a shell builtin
ls is aliased to `ls --color=auto'
Is it a builtin, an alias, or a program on disk?
module avail samtools
On HPC, software is often hidden behind environment modules.






Tip



help cd works for shell builtins that have no man page.




shortcuts — Keyboard shortcuts
These save more time than any alias. Tab completion also prevents typos in long filenames.


syntax

Tab · Ctrl-C · Ctrl-D · Ctrl-R · Ctrl-A / Ctrl-E · ↑ ↓

# Tab        complete a file or command name (press twice to list options)
# Ctrl-C     cancel the running command / abandon the current line
# Ctrl-D     end of input; on an empty prompt it logs you out
# Ctrl-R     search backwards through history
# Ctrl-A / E jump to start / end of line
# Ctrl-L     clear the screen
# Up / Down  previous / next command
Reference, not something to run.
history | tail -n 20
Your last 20 commands.
!!
Re-run the previous command. sudo !! is the classic, but you rarely have sudo on a cluster.






Warning



Ctrl-S freezes terminal output in many terminals. If your screen stops responding, press Ctrl-Q.

title: bash: Advanced commands to work with Linux systems
text:
File navigation
Moving around the filesystem, making and removing things, and finding files on a shared cluster.

pwd — Print working directory
Shows the absolute path of the directory you are in. Run it whenever you are unsure where a relative path will point.


syntax

pwd

pwd
/scratch/ada/project/fastq


ls — List directory contents
Lists files. Flags combine: -lh is the same as -l -h.


syntax

ls [-l] [-a] [-h] [-t] [-r] [PATH...]

ls -lh
-rw-r--r-- 1 ada lab 1.2G Oct  2 09:14 S01_R1.fastq.gz
Long listing with human-readable sizes (K, M, G).
ls -la
Include hidden dotfiles such as .bashrc.
ls -ltr
Sort by time, oldest first, so the newest file ends up next to your prompt.
ls *.vcf.gz
Glob: the shell expands the pattern before ls ever runs.
ls -d */
Directories only.






Tip



Read permissions as owner / group / others: rw-r--r-- means you can write, everyone else can only read.








Warning



ls on a directory with millions of files can hang the shared filesystem. Use ls -f | head or find . -maxdepth 1 | head.




cd — Change directory
Moves you to another directory. With no argument, it takes you home.


syntax

cd [PATH]

cd /scratch/$USER/project
Absolute path: starts with /, works from anywhere.
cd data/raw
Relative path: resolved from where you are now.
cd ..
Up one level. cd ../.. goes up two.
cd ~
Home. Plain cd does the same.
cd -
Back to the previous directory, like a TV remote’s ‘last channel’.
cd "My Data"
Quote names that contain spaces.






Tip



. is the current directory, .. is the parent, ~ is your home, / is the filesystem root.




paths — Absolute vs relative paths
An absolute path starts at / and means the same thing everywhere. A relative path depends on your current directory, which is why scripts that work interactively can fail inside a batch job.


syntax

/abs/path   rel/path   ./file   ../sibling   ~/file

realpath reads.fq
/scratch/ada/project/reads.fq
Turn a relative path into an absolute one.
cd "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"
Inside a Slurm job script: start where you ran sbatch, so relative paths behave.
./run_qc.sh
Run a script in the current directory. The ./ is required because . is not on $PATH.






Warning



~ is not expanded inside quotes: "~/data" is a literal tilde. Use "$HOME/data".




mkdir — Make directories
Creates directories. -p creates parent directories as needed and does not complain if the directory already exists.


syntax

mkdir [-p] DIR...

mkdir results
mkdir -p results/qc/fastqc logs
Nested path plus a second directory in one call.
mkdir -p analysis/{raw,trimmed,aligned}
Brace expansion creates three sibling directories.


cp — Copy files
Copies files. Directories need -r. With several sources, the last argument must be a directory.


syntax

cp [-r] [-i] [-v] SOURCE... DEST

cp config.yaml config.yaml.bak
Quick backup before editing.
cp -r ref/ /scratch/$USER/ref/
Copy a directory tree.
cp -i *.vcf archive/
-i asks before overwriting anything.
rsync -avh --progress data/ /scratch/$USER/data/
For large transfers, rsync resumes and shows progress.






Warning



cp overwrites the destination silently unless you use -i or -n.




mv — Move or rename
Renaming and moving are the same operation. Moving within one filesystem is instant regardless of size.


syntax

mv [-i] [-n] SOURCE... DEST

mv sample1.fq S01_R1.fq
Rename.
mv *.log logs/
Move many files into a directory.
mv -n new.txt old.txt
-n never overwrites an existing file.






Warning



mv a.txt b.txt replaces b.txt without asking if it exists.




rm — Remove files
Deletes files permanently. There is no recycle bin on a cluster, and scratch is usually not backed up.


syntax

rm [-i] [-r] [-f] PATH...

rm tmp.txt
rm -i *.bam
Confirm each deletion.
rm -r old_run/
Remove a directory and everything in it.
ls *.tmp && rm *.tmp
Preview what a glob matches before deleting it.
rmdir empty_dir
Removes only empty directories: a safe default.






Warning



rm -rf $DIR/ with an empty $DIR becomes rm -rf /. Quote and guard: rm -rf "${DIR:?not set}"/.








Warning



A stray space is fatal: rm -rf ./ data deletes the current directory, not ./data.




find — Find files
Recursively searches a directory tree by name, type, size, or age. Quote the pattern so find, not the shell, does the matching.


syntax

find PATH [-name 'PATTERN'] [-type f|d] [-size +N] [-mtime -N]

find . -name '*.fastq.gz'
Every gzipped FASTQ below here.
find /scratch/$USER -type f -size +10G
Large files that are eating your quota.
find . -name '*.log' -mtime -1
Logs modified in the last 24 hours.
find . -maxdepth 1 -type d
Immediate subdirectories only.
find . -name '*.tmp' -print
Always run with -print first; only then swap it for -delete.






Warning



Unquoted find . -name *.txt breaks when the current directory already contains a .txt file, because the shell expands it first.




du / df / quota — Disk usage
Clusters enforce quotas. When writes start failing, these show where your space went.


syntax

du -sh PATH   |   df -h PATH   |   quota -s

du -sh *
Size of each item in the current directory.
du -sh * | sort -h
Same, sorted smallest to largest.
df -h $HOME
Free space on the filesystem holding your home.
quota -s
Your quota on many systems. Some sites use myquota, lfs quota, or a custom command.


ln -s — Symbolic links
A shortcut that points at another path. Useful for linking shared reference genomes into your project without copying them.


syntax

ln -s TARGET LINK_NAME

ln -s /shared/refs/Pinus_taeda_v2.fa ref.fa
ref.fa now points to the shared genome.
ls -l ref.fa
ref.fa -> /shared/refs/Pinus_taeda_v2.fa






Tip



The argument order matches cp: what exists first, then the new name.

title: bash: Advanced commands to work with Linux systems
text:
Core utilities
Look inside files without opening an editor: cat, head, tail, wc, and the small tools you chain them with.

cat — Concatenate & print
Prints whole files to the screen, or joins several files into one stream. Best for small files.


syntax

cat [-n] [-A] FILE...

cat samples.txt
Print a short file.
cat -n samples.txt
Number every line.
cat part1.fq part2.fq > combined.fq
Join files. Order is preserved.
cat -A sheet.csv | head
Show hidden characters: ^M$ at line ends means Windows line endings.






Tip



Gzipped FASTQ files can be concatenated directly: cat a.fq.gz b.fq.gz > ab.fq.gz produces a valid gzip file.








Warning



Running cat on a 50 GB file floods your terminal. Use head or less instead.








Warning



cat with no filename waits for keyboard input. Press Ctrl-D (end) or Ctrl-C (cancel).




head — First lines
Shows the start of a file, 10 lines by default. Ideal for peeking at headers and file formats.


syntax

head [-n N] [-c BYTES] FILE...

head data.csv
First 10 lines.
head -n 4 reads.fastq
One FASTQ record is exactly 4 lines.
head -n -1 data.csv
GNU only: everything except the last line.
zcat reads.fastq.gz | head -n 8
Peek inside a gzipped file without decompressing it to disk.
head -n 1 *.csv
Several files: head prints a ==> name <== banner for each.






Warning



gzip: stdout: Broken pipe after zcat | head is harmless: head simply stopped reading early.




tail — Last lines
Shows the end of a file. -f keeps following it as it grows, which is how you watch a running job’s log.


syntax

tail [-n N] [-n +K] [-f] FILE

tail -n 20 slurm-123456.out
Last 20 lines of a job log.
tail -f slurm-123456.out
Live view. Ctrl-C stops watching; it does not stop the job.
tail -n +2 data.csv
Start at line 2, i.e. drop the header.
head -n 200 data.csv | tail -n 1
Print exactly line 200.


less — Page through a file
Opens a file one screen at a time without loading it all into memory. Safe on huge files.


syntax

less [-S] [-N] FILE

less -S variants.vcf
-S turns off line wrapping; use ← → to scroll wide VCF rows.
zless reads.fastq.gz
Page through a gzipped file.
# inside less:
#   Space / b   page down / up
#   g / G       start / end
#   /pattern    search forward, n = next match
#   q           quit
Keys to remember.


wc — Count lines, words, bytes
Counts lines (-l), words (-w), and bytes (-c). Strictly, -l counts newline characters.


syntax

wc [-l] [-w] [-c] FILE...

wc -l samples.txt
96 samples.txt
Filename is printed after the count.
wc -l < samples.txt
96
Read from stdin instead: you get just the number, handy in scripts.
echo $(( $(zcat reads.fq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))
Number of reads in a FASTQ: lines divided by 4.
grep -vc '^#' variants.vcf
Count variant rows, skipping header lines (grep -c counts matches).
wc -l *.txt
Several files get a ‘total’ line at the end.






Warning



If the last line has no trailing newline, wc -l reports one fewer line than you expect.




sort / uniq — Sort and deduplicate
sort orders lines; uniq collapses adjacent duplicates. Because uniq only looks at neighbors, you almost always sort first.


syntax

sort [-n] [-h] [-r] [-k N] [-t SEP] [-u] FILE   |   uniq [-c] [-d]

sort -k2,2n coords.tsv
Sort numerically on column 2 only.
sort -t, -k3,3 data.csv
Comma-separated: sort on the third field.
cut -f1 calls.tsv | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
Frequency table of column 1, most common first.
sort -u ids.txt
Sort and drop duplicates in one step.






Warning



Without -n, sort is alphabetical: 10 comes before 9.




cut — Extract columns
Pulls out fields from delimited text. The default delimiter is Tab.


syntax

cut -f LIST [-d DELIM] FILE

cut -f1,2 variants.tsv
Columns 1 and 2 of a tab-separated file.
cut -d, -f3- data.csv
Comma-separated, column 3 to the end.
grep -v '^##' variants.vcf | cut -f1-5 | head
Peek at CHROM POS ID REF ALT.






Warning



cut cannot handle quoted CSV fields that contain commas. Use csvcut or R/Python for real CSV.




grep — Search text
Prints lines that match a pattern. Quote the pattern in single quotes so the shell leaves it alone.


syntax

grep [-i] [-v] [-c] [-n] [-w] [-E] [-r] 'PATTERN' FILE...

grep 'ERROR' slurm-*.out
Which job logs mention an error?
grep -c '^>' contigs.fa
Count sequences in a FASTA (lines starting with >).
grep -v '^#' variants.vcf | head
-v inverts: skip header lines.
grep -n -i 'oom' job.log
Case-insensitive, with line numbers.
grep -E 'S0[1-5]_' samples.txt
Extended regular expressions.
zgrep -c 'PASS' calls.vcf.gz
Search inside a gzipped file.






Warning



grep '>' file is fine. grep > file (no quotes) truncates file and grep waits for input.




zcat / gzip — Compressed files
Most sequencing data arrives gzipped. The z-tools let you read it without unpacking to disk.


syntax

zcat FILE.gz   |   gzip [-k] FILE   |   gunzip FILE.gz

zcat reads.fq.gz | head -n 4
First FASTQ record.
gzip -k results.tsv
-k keeps the original file.
gunzip -t reads.fq.gz && echo OK
Test archive integrity after a transfer.
tar -xzf archive.tar.gz
Extract a .tar.gz (x = extract, z = gzip, f = file).

title: bash: Advanced commands to work with Linux systems
text:
Redirection & pipes
Every command has three streams. Redirection decides where they come from and where they go.

Redirection visualizer
Pick an operator. The demo command is ls real.txt missing.txt, which produces one line on stdout and one on stderr.

redir = [
  {"op": "cmd", "stdout": "terminal", "stderr": "terminal", "note": "By default both output streams land on your screen, interleaved."},
  {"op": "cmd > out.txt", "stdout": "out.txt", "stderr": "terminal", "note": "stdout goes to the file (truncated first). Errors still show on screen."},
  {"op": "cmd >> out.txt", "stdout": "out.txt (append)", "stderr": "terminal", "note": "Same as >, but adds to the end of the file."},
  {"op": "cmd < in.txt", "stdout": "terminal", "stderr": "terminal", "note": "The command reads its input from the file instead of the keyboard."},
  {"op": "cmd 2> err.txt", "stdout": "terminal", "stderr": "err.txt", "note": "Only stderr (fd 2) is captured. Normal output still prints."},
  {"op": "cmd > out.txt 2> err.txt", "stdout": "out.txt", "stderr": "err.txt", "note": "Split data from diagnostics: the classic aligner pattern."},
  {"op": "cmd > all.txt 2>&1", "stdout": "all.txt", "stderr": "all.txt", "note": "First point stdout at the file, then make stderr a copy of stdout. Both end up in the file."},
  {"op": "cmd 2>&1 > all.txt", "stdout": "all.txt", "stderr": "terminal", "note": "Trap: stderr copied stdout while stdout was still the terminal. Only stdout reaches the file.", "trap": true},
  {"op": "cmd &> all.txt", "stdout": "all.txt", "stderr": "all.txt", "note": "Bash shorthand for > all.txt 2>&1."},
  {"op": "cmd | next", "stdout": "next (stdin)", "stderr": "terminal", "note": "Only stdout flows down the pipe. Errors bypass it and print to the screen."},
  {"op": "cmd 2>&1 | next", "stdout": "next (stdin)", "stderr": "next (stdin)", "note": "Merge stderr into stdout, then pipe both."},
  {"op": "cmd 2> /dev/null", "stdout": "terminal", "stderr": "/dev/null (discarded)", "note": "Throw errors away. Use sparingly."},
  {"op": "cmd | tee log.txt", "stdout": "terminal + log.txt", "stderr": "terminal", "note": "tee duplicates stdout to the screen and a file."}
]

viewof pick = Inputs.select(redir, {label: "Operator", format: r => r.op, value: redir[6]})

cls = d => /dev\/null/.test(d) ? "" : /next/.test(d) ? "pipe" : /\.txt/.test(d) ? "file" : ""

html`<div class="flow">
  <div class="node">stdout (1)</div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="node ${cls(pick.stdout)}">${pick.stdout}</div>
  <div class="node">stderr (2)</div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="node ${pick.trap ? "bad" : cls(pick.stderr)}">${pick.stderr}</div>
</div>
<p style="border-left:3px solid ${pick.trap ? "#a2401f" : "#1e5a43"}; padding-left:.75rem">${pick.note}</p>`































0 1 2 — The three standard streams
Every process starts with three file descriptors: 0 = stdin (input, normally the keyboard), 1 = stdout (normal output), 2 = stderr (errors and warnings). Both 1 and 2 normally go to your terminal, which is why they look identical until you redirect one.


syntax

0 stdin   1 stdout   2 stderr

ls real.txt missing.txt > out.txt
ls: cannot access 'missing.txt': No such file or directory
The listing goes to out.txt; the error still appears on screen because it is stderr.






Tip



Slurm writes both streams to slurm-JOBID.out by default. Use #SBATCH -o and #SBATCH -e to split them.




> — Write stdout to a file
Sends stdout into a file, creating it if needed and truncating it to zero length first if it exists.


syntax

command > FILE

ls *.bam > bam_list.txt
set -o noclobber
Protect yourself: now > refuses to overwrite existing files. Use >| to force.






Warning



The file is truncated before the command runs. sort data.txt > data.txt leaves you with an empty file.




>> — Append stdout
Adds to the end of a file instead of replacing it.


syntax

command >> FILE

echo "$(date) started $SAMPLE" >> run.log
Build up a log across many commands.
for f in *.csv; do tail -n +2 "$f" >> merged.csv; done
Append every file minus its header.






Warning



Rerunning an appending script doubles the output. Clear the file first with > merged.csv if needed.




< — Read stdin from a file
Feeds a file into a command’s standard input. The command sees data but not a filename.


syntax

command < FILE

wc -l < samples.txt
96
Prints only the count, with no filename.
while read -r id; do echo "processing $id"; done < samples.txt
Loop over lines of a file.


2> / 2>&1 / &> — Redirect errors
Put a file descriptor number before the operator to redirect that stream. 2>&1 means ‘make stderr go wherever stdout currently goes’.


syntax

cmd 2> err.txt   |   cmd > all.txt 2>&1   |   cmd &> all.txt

bwa mem ref.fa r1.fq r2.fq > aln.sam 2> bwa.log
Data to one file, messages to another: the standard bioinformatics pattern.
./pipeline.sh > run.log 2>&1
Both streams into one file. Order matters: file first, then 2>&1.
./pipeline.sh &> run.log
Bash shorthand for the line above.
find / -name '*.fa' 2> /dev/null
Discard the permission-denied noise.






Warning



cmd 2>&1 > file is not the same as cmd > file 2>&1. Redirections run left to right; in the first form stderr copies stdout while it still points at the terminal.




| — Pipes
Connects one command’s stdout to the next command’s stdin. Nothing touches the disk in between.


syntax

cmd1 | cmd2 | cmd3

zcat reads.fq.gz | head -n 400000 | gzip > subset.fq.gz
Take the first 100,000 reads.
grep -v '^#' calls.vcf | cut -f1 | sort | uniq -c
Variants per chromosome.
cmd 2>&1 | less
Pipes only carry stdout. Merge stderr first if you want to page through errors too.
set -o pipefail
In scripts: make a pipeline fail if any stage fails, not just the last one.


tee — Split output: screen and file
Copies stdin to a file and to stdout, so you can watch output and save it at the same time.


syntax

cmd | tee [-a] FILE

./qc.sh 2>&1 | tee qc.log
Watch it live and keep a log.
./qc.sh | tee -a qc.log
-a appends instead of overwriting.


/dev/null — The bit bucket
A special file that discards anything written to it and is always empty when read.


syntax

cmd > /dev/null 2>&1

command -v samtools > /dev/null || echo 'load the samtools module first'
Check that a tool exists, without printing its path.
grep -q 'PASS' calls.vcf && echo found
grep -q is a cleaner way to stay silent.






Warning



Silencing stderr also hides real errors. Do it only when you know what you are throwing away.




<< EOF — Here-documents
Feeds a block of inline text to a command’s stdin. Quoting the delimiter ('EOF') turns off variable expansion inside the block.


syntax

cmd << EOF ... EOF   |   cmd << 'EOF' ... EOF

cat > samples.txt << EOF
S01
S02
S03
EOF
Write a small file without opening an editor.
cat > job.sh << 'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH -t 01:00:00
echo "running on $HOSTNAME"
EOF
Quoted delimiter: $HOSTNAME is written literally and expanded later, on the compute node.
grep -c x <<< "$SEQ"
Here-string: feed a single variable as stdin.






Warning



The closing EOF must be alone on its line with no leading spaces (unless you use <<- with tabs).




<( ) — Process substitution
Treats a command’s output as if it were a file. Great for tools that demand filenames.


syntax

cmd <(other_cmd) <(other_cmd)

diff <(sort a.txt) <(sort b.txt)
Compare two files ignoring order.
comm -12 <(sort ids_a.txt) <(sort ids_b.txt)
IDs present in both lists.
paste <(cut -f1 a.tsv) <(cut -f3 b.tsv)
Glue columns from two files side by side.






Warning



Bash only. It fails in sh with syntax error near unexpected token '('.

title: bash: Advanced commands to work with Linux systems
text:
Quoting rules
Quotes decide what the shell expands and where it splits words. Most mysterious bugs start here.

'...' — Single quotes: fully literal
Everything between single quotes is taken exactly as typed. No variables, no globs, no backslash escapes. You cannot put a single quote inside single quotes.


syntax

'literal text'

echo 'Cost: $5 * 3'
Cost: $5 * 3
grep -E '^chr[0-9]+\s' file.bed
The safe default for regular expressions.
awk '{print $1}' data.tsv
Single quotes protect awk’s own $1 from the shell.
echo 'It'\''s done'
It's done
To include a quote: close, add an escaped quote, reopen.


"..." — Double quotes: expand, but do not split
Variables ($VAR) and command substitution ($(...)) still expand, but the result stays one word, and globs are not expanded. Inside, a backslash only escapes $, backtick, ", and \.


syntax

"text with $VAR and $(cmd)"

FILE="my reads.fq"
wc -l "$FILE"
Without quotes, wc would look for two files: my and reads.fq.
echo "Home is $HOME, today is $(date +%F)"
Home is /home/ada, today is 2026-10-05
echo "Price: \$5"
Price: $5
Escape a literal dollar.






Tip



Rule of thumb: always double-quote variable expansions, "$var", unless you specifically want splitting.




\ — Backslash escapes
Outside quotes, a backslash makes the next single character literal. At the end of a line it continues the command onto the next line.


syntax

\CHAR   |   long command \

ls My\ Data/
Escape a space (Tab completion does this for you).
sbatch --job-name=qc \
       --time=02:00:00 \
       --mem=8G run.sh
Split a long command over lines.






Warning



A space after the trailing backslash breaks line continuation, and the error is almost invisible.




$VAR ${VAR} — Variables
Assign with no spaces around =. Use braces when the name is followed by characters that could be part of a name.


syntax

NAME=value   "$NAME"   "${NAME}_suffix"

SAMPLE=S01
echo "${SAMPLE}_R1.fq"
S01_R1.fq
Without braces, bash looks for a variable named SAMPLE_R1.
OUT=${OUT:-results}
Default value if OUT is unset or empty.
f=reads.fastq.gz
echo "${f%.fastq.gz}"
reads
Strip a suffix: a clean way to build output names.
export THREADS=8
export makes the variable visible to programs you launch.






Warning



NAME = value (with spaces) runs a command called NAME. Bash replies NAME: command not found.




$( ) — Command substitution
Runs a command and pastes its output in place. Prefer $(...) over old-style backticks because it nests and reads clearly.


syntax

"$(command)"

N=$(wc -l < samples.txt)
echo "There are $N samples"
There are 96 samples
mkdir "run_$(date +%Y%m%d)"
Date-stamped output directory.
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID on $(hostname)"


* ? [ ] — Globs (wildcards)
Unquoted *, ?, and [...] are expanded by the shell into matching filenames before the command runs. Quoting turns them back into literal characters.


syntax

*  any string   ?  one char   [abc]  one of   {a,b}  brace list

ls S0?_R1.fq.gz
S01 to S09, but not S10.
ls *_R[12].fq.gz
Both read pairs.
echo *.fasta
*.fasta
If nothing matches, bash passes the literal text *.fasta.
echo '*.fasta'
*.fasta
Quoted: never expanded.
for f in *.fq.gz; do echo "$f"; done
Loop over files the safe way. Never parse ls output.






Tip



{a,b} brace expansion is not a glob: it always expands, whether or not files exist.




spaces — Spaces in filenames
The shell splits words on spaces. A name like Field Notes.txt becomes two arguments unless you quote or escape it. Easiest fix: avoid spaces in names you create.


syntax

"Field Notes.txt"   'Field Notes.txt'   Field\ Notes.txt

cat "Field Notes.txt"
for f in *.txt; do mv "$f" "${f// /_}"; done
Replace spaces with underscores in every .txt filename.
find . -name '*.txt' -print0 | xargs -0 wc -l
-print0 and -0 keep odd filenames intact through a pipe.


nested — Quoting across ssh & sbatch --wrap
When a command string is handed to another shell, it is parsed twice: once locally, once remotely. Choose the outer quote type based on where you want variables to expand.


syntax

ssh host 'cmd $REMOTE_VAR'   |   sbatch --wrap "cmd $LOCAL_VAR"

ssh cluster 'echo $HOSTNAME'
login01
Single quotes: expanded on the remote machine.
ssh cluster "echo $HOSTNAME"
my-laptop
Double quotes: expanded locally before sending.
sbatch --wrap="gzip -k '$PWD/big file.tsv'"
Outer double quotes expand $PWD now; inner single quotes protect the space later.

title: bash: Advanced commands to work with Linux systems
text:
Beginner errors, decoded
Click an error to expand it. Tip: press / or s to open site search and paste part of an error message.






Importantcommand not found





-bash: samtools: command not found
What it means. The program is not on your $PATH. On a cluster this usually means its module is not loaded. It can also be a typo, or a script in the current directory run without ./
Fix.
module avail samtools
module load samtools
./myscript.sh        # not just myscript.sh









ImportantNo such file or directory





head: cannot open 'Reads.fq' for reading: No such file or directory
What it means. Wrong path, wrong case (Linux is case-sensitive), or a relative path resolved from a different directory than you thought. Also appears when a glob matches nothing and is passed through literally.
Fix.
pwd
ls -l
realpath reads.fq









ImportantPermission denied





-bash: ./run.sh: Permission denied
What it means. Either the script lacks the execute bit, or you are trying to write into a directory you do not own (for example a shared reference folder or another user’s home).
Fix.
chmod +x run.sh
bash run.sh          # or run it via bash directly
ls -ld /shared/refs  # check directory permissions









ImportantIs a directory





cat: results: Is a directory
What it means. You gave a directory where a file was expected.
Fix.
ls results/
cat results/summary.txt









Important-r not specified; omitting directory





cp: -r not specified; omitting directory 'ref'
What it means. cp copies files only, unless told to recurse into directories.
Fix.
cp -r ref/ backup_ref/









Important> prompt that will not go away





>
>
>
What it means. The shell is waiting for you to finish an unclosed quote, bracket, or here-document. It is not frozen.
Fix.
# Press Ctrl-C to cancel the line, then retype it with balanced quotes
echo "done"









Importantunexpected EOF while looking for matching





line 12: unexpected EOF while looking for matching `"'
What it means. A script has an unclosed quote somewhere above the line reported. Bash only notices at the end of the file.
Fix.
bash -n script.sh     # syntax check without running
grep -n '"' script.sh   # find the odd one out









Importantambiguous redirect





-bash: $OUT: ambiguous redirect
What it means. The redirection target is an unquoted variable that is empty or contains spaces, so it does not expand to exactly one filename.
Fix.
echo "[$OUT]"         # inspect it
cmd > "$OUT"









Important[: too many arguments





-bash: [: too many arguments
What it means. An unquoted variable inside a test contained spaces and was split into several words.
Fix.
if [ "$name" = "S01 rep1" ]; then echo match; fi
# or use [[ ]] which does not split
if [[ $name == "S01 rep1" ]]; then echo match; fi









ImportantFile is empty after sort/cat/grep





$ sort data.txt > data.txt
$ wc -l data.txt
0 data.txt
What it means. The shell truncates the output file before the command starts reading the same file. The data is gone.
Fix.
sort data.txt > data.sorted.txt && mv data.sorted.txt data.txt
sort -o data.txt data.txt     # sort can do it safely itself









Importantbad interpreter: /bin/bash^M





-bash: ./run.sh: /bin/bash^M: bad interpreter: No such file or directory
What it means. The script was edited on Windows and has CRLF line endings. The invisible ecomes part of every line.
Fix.
cat -A run.sh | head -n 2   # shows ^M$ at line ends
sed -i 's/\r$//' run.sh       # or: dos2unix run.sh









Importantevent not found





-bash: !nice: event not found
What it means. In interactive bash, ! inside double quotes triggers history expansion.
Fix.
echo 'Job done!nice'     # single quotes
set +H                   # or turn history expansion off









ImportantNAME: command not found (on assignment)





-bash: THREADS: command not found
What it means. Spaces around = turn a variable assignment into a command named THREADS with arguments = and 8.
Fix.
THREADS=8









ImportantArgument list too long





-bash: /bin/rm: Argument list too long
What it means. A glob such as *.tmp expanded to more filenames than the kernel allows in a single command.
Fix.
find . -name '*.tmp' -delete
# or process in batches
find . -name '*.fq' -print0 | xargs -0 gzip









ImportantDisk quota exceeded





cp: error writing 'big.bam': Disk quota exceeded
What it means. You hit your storage or file-count limit, usually in $HOME, which tends to be small on clusters.
Fix.
quota -s
du -sh ~/* | sort -h | tail
mv ~/big_run /scratch/$USER/









ImportantKilled





Killed
What it means. The process was terminated, often for using too much memory on a login node, or (inside a job) for exceeding the memory you requested. Slurm logs show oom-kill or OUT_OF_MEMORY.
Fix.
srun --mem=16G --time=01:00:00 --pty bash   # interactive compute node
sacct -j JOBID --format=JobID,State,MaxRSS,ReqMem









ImportantTerminal hangs after cat or grep





$ cat
_
What it means. You ran a command that reads stdin without giving it a file, so it is waiting for you to type. Common after a missing filename, or after grep pattern > file with no input file.
Fix.
# Ctrl-D to send end-of-input, or Ctrl-C to cancel
grep 'pattern' input.txt > hits.txt









Importantgzip: stdout: Broken pipe





gzip: stdout: Broken pipe
What it means. Harmless. head or less stopped reading early, so the upstream command was told to stop.
Fix.
zcat reads.fq.gz 2>/dev/null | head









Importantsyntax error near unexpected token(’`





sh: syntax error near unexpected token `('
What it means. You used a bash-only feature, such as <( ) or arrays, in a script run by sh, or you have an unquoted parenthesis in a filename.
Fix.
bash script.sh            # not: sh script.sh
#!/bin/bash                # first line of the script
ls "sample (copy).txt"

title: bash: Advanced commands to work with Linux systems
text:
Quick reference


Navigate



Command
Does




pwd
where am I


ls -lh
list with sizes


cd DIR
go to DIR


cd ..
up one


cd -
previous dir


cd
home


realpath F
absolute path





Manage



Command
Does




mkdir -p a/b
make nested dirs


cp -r SRC DST
copy (dirs need -r)


mv OLD NEW
move / rename


rm -i F
delete, ask first


ln -s T L
symlink


find . -name '*.x'
find by name


du -sh *
sizes here





Inspect



Command
Does




cat F
print file


head -n N F
first N lines


tail -n N F
last N lines


tail -n +2 F
skip header


tail -f LOG
follow log


less -S F
page, no wrap


wc -l F
count lines





Filter



Command
Does




grep 'p' F
matching lines


grep -v 'p'
non-matching


grep -c 'p'
count matches


cut -f1,3
columns (tab)


sort -k2,2n
sort numeric col 2


uniq -c
count adjacent dupes


zcat F.gz
read gzip





Redirect



Command
Does




> F
stdout to F (overwrite)


>> F
stdout append


< F
stdin from F


2> F
stderr to F


> F 2>&1
both to F


&> F
both (bash)


a | b
stdout of a into b


| tee F
screen + file


2> /dev/null
discard errors





Quote



Command
Does




'...'
literal, nothing expands


"..."
expand $ but keep one word


\x
escape one char


"$VAR"
always quote vars


"${V}_x"
braces before text


"$(cmd)"
insert output


'*.txt'
stop glob expansion





Keys



Command
Does




Tab
complete


Ctrl-C

Ctrl-D
end input / logout


Ctrl-R

Ctrl-A / E

q
quit less / man

title: bash: Module 2 Scripting and automation on HPC systems
text:
Cluster exercise: turn the red-spruce download into a re-runnable, self-checking workflow
In the introductory module you typed commands one at a time. That is how everyone learns, but it does not scale: you cannot remember exactly what you typed three weeks ago, a collaborator cannot rerun it, and a typo in step 4 silently ruins step 9.
In this module you will put those same steps into Bash scripts that check their own work, stop on errors, record what they did, and can be run again safely. Along the way you will process many files at once, verify data with checksums, move files on and off the cluster, set permissions for a shared lab directory, and submit your first Slurm job array.
You will keep working in the same cluster-exercise/ project and the same red-spruce fitness-trait dataset.
